note: RE-MEASURE of all 144 quadruped mammals after waves 7-13. Compare to the pre-wave-7 run: unique heads were 20/141.

rows.readsAs: An elephant — unmistakable, though a slightly deflated cartoon one
rows.headWhy: The trunk plus the small forward-set eye high on a domed cranium makes this head impossible to confuse with anything else in the batch. What it does NOT deliver is the Asian-specific read: the forehead is one smooth dome, not twin domes with a dip, and the ear is a large soft-cornered oval blob (an African-sized ear) rather than a small triangular flap. The trunk tapers to a plain rounded tube with no single dorsal lip at the tip.
rows.defect: The legs are far too slender — they are the same pencil-thin tubes used on the camel and banteng in this batch, roughly 1/9 the body depth, so a 4-tonne animal is standing on deer legs. There is no visible knee/elbow mass and the columns do not flare into the foot; the foot is a small dark cap with toenails glued to the bottom of a straight tube. The torso also carries an unexplained pale seam running from the shoulder to the belly that reads as a separate pasted-on panel rather than a plane change on the solid.
rows.fix: Rebuild the limbs as weight-bearing pillars: at least 2.5x the current width, near-vertical, widening slightly at the ground into a rounded circular foot pad with nails set into its front rim rather than under the tube. Shorten the leg length so the belly line drops closer to the elbow. Replace the oval ear with a smaller triangle whose top edge is a straight fold at the skull and whose bottom comes to a soft point; add a shallow medial notch across the cranium to produce the twin-dome profile, and finish the trunk with a single forward-projecting lip at the tip.

rows.readsAs: A camel — the long S-neck and drooping muzzle sell it immediately
rows.headWhy: Specific: a small head on a long curved neck, with a convex Roman muzzle, a downturned lip line, a low-set nostril and a tiny ear tucked behind the eye. Nothing else in the batch has this profile. Weakness: the ear is a plain dark triangle with no fur fringe, and the eye lacks the heavy hooded lid and long lashes that are the camel's other signature.
rows.defect: The two humps are not part of the animal. They are two separate rounded ovals in a slightly different tone, sitting ON the topline like eggs placed on a table — no fairing into the back, no shared silhouette, and the gap between them cuts all the way down to the spine line. The flank additionally has two large lighter oval patches with visible edges that look like pasted decals rather than shoulder and haunch masses. And the mustRead shaggy hair is entirely absent: neck, chest, throat and hump crowns are all smooth airbrushed tan.
rows.fix: Model the humps as fat deposits growing out of the dorsal solid — merge their bases into the back so the silhouette is one continuous topline with two peaks and a shallow saddle between them, not two detached domes. Kill the two oval flank decals; if shoulder and haunch mass is wanted, express it with form shading on the torso solid, not with edged shapes. Then add the winter coat: a hanging fringe along the underside of the neck and chest, and a darker shaggy cap of hair breaking the outline at the crown of each hump.

rows.readsAs: A striped plank on four pipes — closest guess would be a toy zebra or a crudely painted ottoman, not a living animal
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is a small rounded wedge with a circular ear and a dark-and-pale smudge where the face mask should be. There is no long tapering badger snout, and critically the white stripe does not run back over the crown — the facial markings read as random mottling. Swap this head onto the beaver or the bear and nobody in the room would flag it.
rows.defect: Three hard anatomy failures. (1) The torso is a rectangular slab with near-square corners and a dead-straight flat top and bottom — no shoulder, no haunch, no belly curve; it is a box, not a solid animal. (2) The coat stripes run VERTICALLY as a dense black barcode across the back, which is the exact opposite of the badger's longitudinal head stripe, and they stop at a hard edge mid-body. (3) The legs are open-ended cylinders — you can see the elliptical cut face where each tube meets the ground, like sawn-off pipe. There are no feet and no long straight digging foreclaws at all. The whole animal is also drawn small and floats high in the frame with the shadow detached below it.
rows.fix: Rebuild the body as a low-slung wedge that is widest and deepest at the shoulders and tapers to the hips, with a convex back and a belly that nearly touches the ground — kill every straight edge and corner. Remove the vertical barcode entirely; replace it with grizzled grey flank fur and put the ONE white stripe where it belongs, starting at the nose and running back between the eyes over the crown, flanked by two black eye bands. Cap the leg tubes with a broad flat forepaw and give the front feet five long straight pale claws projecting forward past the toes. Re-scale the subject to fill the frame and re-seat the shadow under the feet.

rows.readsAs: A brown cow with a white horseshoe stuck to its face
rows.headWhy: Unique only by accident. The white crescent over the muzzle is unlike anything else in the batch, so it would be noticed if swapped — but it reads as a piece of hardware pasted on top of the head, not as horns. The two horns are fused into one continuous ring that arcs DOWN across the bridge of the nose and occludes the eye, instead of two separate horns rising from the skull's outer corners and sweeping up and back. Behind it, the actual head is a plain blunt bovine wedge with two small dark ears — completely generic.
rows.defect: The horns are the main failure: a single closed white U-shape lying in front of the face, crossing the muzzle and hiding the eye, with no root at the skull and no bald forehead plate joining them. Beyond that, every diagnostic marking is missing — no white rump patch, no white stockings on the lower legs (the legs are uniform brown into black hooves), no white band above the muzzle. The torso also carries the same pasted lighter oval patches as the camel, with visible edges on the shoulder and haunch.
rows.fix: Split the horn into two: anchor each at the outer top corner of the skull, sweep them outward then up and slightly back in a smooth crescent, keep them entirely clear of the muzzle and the eye, and join their bases with a pale bald forehead plate. Then add the species markings — a clean white patch across the rump and under the tail, four white stockings from the knee/hock down to the hoof, and a narrow white band ringing the muzzle above the lip. Blend the flank ovals into the torso shading instead of leaving hard edges.

rows.readsAs: A hay bale or a bristly gourd standing on two wooden blocks, with a small dog head attached
rows.headWhy: Generic. A short rounded lozenge with one small round ear, a dot eye and a black nose bead — that is the same head vocabulary as the beaver in this batch, at a slightly different scale. The dished forehead the reference calls for is absent (the profile from brow to nose is a straight ramp), and the head is far too small relative to the body, so it reads as a decoration rather than the mass it should be.
rows.defect: The mass is in the wrong place: the topline peaks over the HINDQUARTERS and slopes down to the shoulder, which is backwards — there is no muscular shoulder hump over the forelegs at all. The legs are literal rectangular boxes with parallel hard vertical edges and square corners, no taper, no joint, and only two are legible; the paws are dark wedges with a row of white dots for claws, sitting on the front of the block rather than the animal standing on a flat sole. And the coat is treated as straight bristles radiating outward from the rear half of the outline like a hedgehog, while the entire front half of the body is smooth — two different animals in one silhouette.
rows.fix: Move the mass forward: build a distinct muscular hump over the forelegs so the topline is highest at the withers and falls away to a lower rump. Replace the box legs with tapered columns that widen at the shoulder and thigh, narrow at the wrist and hock, and end in a plantigrade sole — a long flat foot printing its whole length on the ground, with five short claws at the toe edge. Delete the radiating bristles and carry a consistent fur treatment around the full silhouette, breaking the outline evenly rather than only on the rump. Enlarge the head, dish the forehead so the brow steps down to the muzzle, and set the small round ears wide on a broad cranium.

rows.readsAs: An otter or a marmot wearing a pale tan sleeve, with a beaver tail attached
rows.headWhy: Generic. Round cranium, one small round ear, a large glossy eye and a blunt dark muzzle — swap it with the bear's head and the only tell would be the size. The single most identifying beaver feature, the pair of big orange chisel incisors, is nowhere in the pixels; the mouth is a plain dark muzzle with no teeth, no lip line and no heavy jaw muscle.
rows.defect: The torso is a pale tan cylinder with horizontal banding that does not match the darker brown of the head, limbs and tail — it reads as a separate sleeve slipped over the animal, with a visible tonal seam at the neck and at the hip. The tail is correct in shape and crosshatch but is attached wrong: it hangs off a short stub limb high on the flank, well above and behind the hips, instead of continuing from the base of the spine. The legs are four identical short rounded stubs with no feet — no broad webbed hind foot, no small grasping forepaw — and the body lacks the humped arched back the reference calls for; the topline is flat.
rows.fix: Unify the coat tone across torso, head and limbs so the body reads as one animal, and remove the horizontal banding seam. Re-root the paddle tail directly at the base of the spine, level with the hips, with the fur transitioning into the scaly surface rather than a stub bridging them. Arch the back into a distinct hump over the hindquarters. Differentiate the feet: small five-fingered forepaws held close under the chest, large splayed webbed hind feet flat on the ground. And put the orange incisors in — two prominent chisel teeth at the front of the muzzle, visible against a shorter upper lip.

rows.readsAs: A shaggy sheep or a scruffy goat — nobody would say bison
rows.headWhy: Generic and actively wrong for the species. The head is small, carried HIGH on a raised neck, with a long narrow tapering muzzle and a big glossy eye — that is an ovine head. A bison head is enormous, hangs LOW below the line of the shoulders, and carries a black beard, a woolly forehead cap and two short upcurved horns. There are no horns, no beard, no forehead wool. Put this head on the banteng with the horns removed and nobody would notice.
rows.defect: The defining silhouette is missing entirely — this is exactly the uniform-barrel failure the reference note warns against. The topline is level from neck to tail with no shoulder hump whatsoever, the hindquarters are the same depth as the forequarters instead of narrow and tapering, and the head is held above the topline instead of below it. The shaggy coat is again drawn as isolated straight bristles poking out around the perimeter of an otherwise smooth body rather than as a mass of hair with its own silhouette, and the pale scribbled strokes across the flank read as scratches on the paint.
rows.fix: Rebuild the topline: a tall muscular hump peaking directly over the forelegs, then a steep continuous slope down to small narrow hips, so the animal is unmistakably front-heavy in silhouette. Drop the head low — the crown should sit at or below the level of the back — and enlarge it to a broad blunt mass with a woolly forehead, a hanging black chin beard, and two short black horns curving up and inward from the sides of the skull. Divide the coat into two zones: a thick woolly cape over the head, hump, shoulders and forelegs whose OUTLINE is ragged, and short smooth hair over the loins and hindquarters — instead of uniform bristles sprayed around the whole edge.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat kid or a young calf with paw-print stickers on it
rows.headWhy: Generic. Small tan ball head, one flat disc ear, one ringed eye, and a stub muzzle — it is the same head as the Cougar's with a different ear disc. Nothing cat about it: no broad cheek ruff, no short deep jaw, no long upper canines or dark lip line, no low-set forward-facing eye pair. Swap it onto the Cougar and nobody would notice.
rows.defect: Nearly every mustRead is missing. (1) The tail is a short upward stub roughly 20% of body length; the clouded leopard's tail equals head+body combined and is the species' single most recognisable feature — the note in the row warns about exactly this error and the render commits it. (2) The blotches are small, uniform, dark paw-print-shaped dots scattered like a cheetah/leopard; there are no large irregular cloud-shaped patches with a dark rim and a paler interior, and no size gradient (big cloud shapes over the flank, small solid spots on the limbs and face). (3) The legs are four identical straight tubes with a slightly darker tip and no paw — no toes, no broad forefoot, no pad. A clouded leopard has very short heavy legs and big paws; here the legs are long and the feet do not exist. (4) The neck rises to a horse-like carriage and the head is held above the shoulder line; a cat's head sits at or below the shoulder on a level neck.
rows.fix: Draw the tail as a thick, evenly-thick, low-carried rope the same length as nose-to-rump, sweeping back and down past the hocks with a subtle ringed pattern — length is the identity, so measure it against the body before shading. Replace the spot generator for this species with a two-tone cloud pattern: large irregular closed shapes (10-20% of torso height each) with a dark brown border and a mid-tan fill, flowing along the flank in an ovoid chain, shrinking to solid dots only on the head and lower limbs. Shorten the legs by about a third and terminate each in a real cat paw — a wide rounded forefoot with 3-4 visible toe lobes, wider than the leg above it. Drop the head so the skull top is level with the shoulder, shorten and deepen the muzzle, put both eyes forward on the face, and give it the cat's rounded low-set ears rather than the current single flat disc.

rows.readsAs: A pale beige dog or a generic marten standing still
rows.headWhy: Generic. A tan wedge with one dark round ear and one oversized white-sclera cartoon eye — the same head part used on the Colugo. The one feature that makes a coati a coati, the long flexible upturned pig-like snout, is absent; the muzzle is a short blunt cone that ends level. Put this head on the Colugo body and the swap would be invisible.
rows.defect: All three mustReads fail. (1) The snout is short, straight and blunt with no upward hook at the tip and no visible mobile nose pad — the coati's defining trait. (2) The tail is short, thick, curled downward and tucked behind the haunch, ending near the hock; it must be at least as long as the body and held vertically like a flagpole, and the banding is a single vague dark smear rather than distinct alternating rings. (3) The feet are plain rounded tube-ends; there are no plantigrade soles, no toes, no long digging claws, and the animal stands high on its toes instead of flat on its heels. The body is also a generic barrel with two lighter airbrushed discs marking shoulder and haunch — the same torso solid as the Cougar and Colugo in this batch — rather than the long, low, arch-backed coati profile.
rows.fix: Rebuild the muzzle as a long tapering tube that bends upward through the last 25% of its length, tipped with a distinct dark rubbery nose disc that overhangs the jaw. Re-rig the tail as a straight vertical mast, body-length or longer, rising from the rump with 6-8 hard-edged alternating dark/light bands. Replace the leg terminations with plantigrade feet: draw the metatarsal sole flat on the ground so the whole foot from heel to toe touches, add five toes and short curved claws, and lower the hindquarters so the back arches gently down toward the shoulders. Lengthen the torso and reduce its depth so the silhouette is long and low, not the standing-calf box currently used.

rows.readsAs: A small mottled lamb or goat kid, standing on four legs
rows.headWhy: Generic. Grey-tan ball, one round dark ear, one modestly-sized white eye with a dark pupil — the identical head component as the Coati. The row calls for huge round forward-facing eyes taking up much of the face; the eye here is a normal side-mounted quadruped eye at ordinary scale. Nothing distinguishes it from the other heads in this batch.
rows.defect: The single most important feature of the animal — the patagium — is entirely absent, and the posture field says 'flying' while the render is a four-legged standing quadruped with a lamb silhouette. There is no membrane between neck and forelimb, none between the fingers, none between hind limb and tail, and the tail is a bare curled stub hanging free. Legs are four separate tubes with plain rounded ends, no elongated fingers and no gripping claws. The mottling is a scatter of brown blobs on a plain ground, not lichen-camouflage: no green-grey ground tone, no soft-edged flecking, no dark speckle over pale patches. The eyes are not enlarged.
rows.fix: This one needs a different pose, not a patch. Render it clinging to a vertical trunk or in a spread glide, seen from the side or three-quarter front, with the patagium drawn as one continuous sheet of skin: a single closed outline running from behind the ear down the neck, out along the forelimb to the fingertips, back along the flank to the hind foot, and then across to enclose the tail all the way to its tip — the completely enclosed tail is what separates it from a flying squirrel, so it must not be left outside the membrane. Show the elongated finger and toe bones as faint darker struts fanning through the membrane. Enlarge the eyes to roughly a third of head height each, place them side by side facing the viewer, and give each a wide dark round pupil. Repaint the coat as soft-edged blotchy lichen camo: mossy grey-green ground with irregular pale patches and fine dark speckling that reads as bark.

rows.readsAs: A tan calf or a smooth beige goat
rows.headWhy: Generic. This is the Clouded Leopard's head in a different colourway — same small tan ball, same single flat ring-shaped ear disc, same ringed eye, same short cone muzzle. There is no small round cat skull, no black muzzle bars, no dark lip line, no white chin, no forward-set binocular eye pair. Swapping it with the Clouded Leopard would go unnoticed.
rows.defect: (1) The tail is a short thin upward-curling stub about a fifth of body length with no black tip — the cougar's tail is very long, thick and heavy, carried low with a distinct black tip, and it is the animal's main field mark. (2) The mustRead 'completely plain unmarked tawny coat' is technically met but the body carries two conspicuous pale airbrushed discs at the shoulder and haunch plus horizontal banding, which read as painted-on markings and break the plainness the row calls out as the identity. (3) The hindquarters sit lower than the shoulders; the note explicitly says the rump should stand higher than the shoulder. (4) The feet are plain tube-ends with dark caps, no paws or toes. (5) The head is carried high on an upright neck, an ungulate posture, not a cat's level low-slung carriage.
rows.fix: Give it a long heavy low-slung tail, nose-to-rump in length or close to it, thick at the base, drooping in a shallow J behind the hocks with a clearly black last fifth. Remove the shoulder/haunch highlight discs and the horizontal banding and let the body be one uniform tawny value with only a soft belly lightening — for this species the absence of markings is the read. Raise the pelvis so the top line rises from shoulder to rump. Terminate the legs in broad round cat paws with 3-4 toe lobes, wider than the leg shaft. Rebuild the head as a small round skull on a level neck at shoulder height, with the black bars framing a pale muzzle, a white chin patch, and both eyes set forward on the face.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat, or a piebald pony
rows.headWhy: Distinct within this batch — it is the only head with a matched pair of upright grey leaf ears, a drawn mouth line and a long down-turned muzzle, so a swap onto any other body would be spotted. But it is distinct in the wrong direction: the profile is caprine. The muzzle tapers to a point instead of ending in a broad blunt square nose pad, there are no horn buds or poll, the forehead is narrow, and the ears point up rather than sitting out sideways as the row requires.
rows.defect: The body reads goat, not cow. (1) No udder at all — the row lists it as a mustRead and the belly line is smooth and tucked up. (2) No dewlap; the throat is a clean straight line from jaw to chest where a cow carries a deep hanging fold. (3) The barrel does not sag: the belly is drawn tight and shallow with two pale airbrushed haunch discs, so the animal is slim-waisted where a cow's gut should swing low and wide, deepest behind the ribs. (4) The ears are set on top of the skull and point upward rather than projecting sideways from behind the eyes. (5) The tail is a thin whip ending in a small grey paddle rather than a long switch with a proper hair tuft. (6) The blotches are small and evenly scattered like a dalmatian's; Holstein patches are large, few and irregular, running over the topline and down the flank.
rows.fix: Deepen and drop the belly line so the barrel sags below the elbow and is deepest just ahead of the stifle, and hang a small four-teat udder between the hind legs against the rear of the belly. Add a dewlap as a hanging triangular fold of skin from the jaw down the throat to the brisket. Re-anchor the ears low on the skull behind and below the eye line, pointing outward and slightly down, roughly horizontal in profile. Square off the muzzle into a broad blunt nose pad with visible nostrils and widen the forehead between the ears. Replace the tail tip paddle with a real switch — a hanging tuft of long strands. Redraw the coat as 4-6 large irregular patches with soft-fingered edges that cross the spine and the shoulder, rather than many small dots.

rows.readsAs: A small pale horse or donkey with a feather duster tied to its rump
rows.headWhy: Generic. Small pale wedge with a long thin tapering muzzle, one dark rounded ear and one white eye — it reads as an equine head and is close enough to the Cow's head minus the leaf ears that a swap would barely register. The mustRead calls for large erect triangular ears, which are the single strongest coyote silhouette cue; what is drawn is a small dark rounded lobe. No black nose pad, no lip line, no canid stop between forehead and muzzle.
rows.defect: (1) The ears are far too small and rounded — they should be tall, erect, sharply triangular and roughly a third of head length, set wide on the skull. (2) The tail is wrong in shape, texture and carriage: it is rendered as a flat striped fan or feather held out horizontally at rump height, where a coyote's is a cylindrical bushy brush hanging DOWN toward the hocks with a black tip — the row's note flags the carriage specifically. (3) The legs end in dark rounded hoof-like caps with no toes, no pads and no claws; they should be compact digitigrade paws with four toes. (4) The build is too tall and too short-bodied, with a level equine topline and a high-carried head on a vertical neck; a coyote is long-bodied and low, with the head carried forward at roughly shoulder height. (5) The muzzle is a smooth cone that merges into the forehead with no stop and no jawline.
rows.fix: Rebuild the ears as two tall pointed triangles standing straight up from the top of the skull, with a visible inner fold and pale inner surface, each about a third of the head's length. Redraw the tail as a thick cylindrical brush of overlapping fur strokes, hanging down and back from the rump to below the hock, tapering to a dark tip — kill the flat striped fan entirely. Replace the hoof caps with small oval digitigrade paws showing four toes and short blunt claws. Lengthen the torso, drop the chest, and lower the neck so the head reaches forward rather than up. Add a canid stop above the eyes so the forehead meets the muzzle at an angle, narrow the muzzle to a wedge, and finish it with a black nose pad and a dark lip line.

rows.readsAs: A deer — a young spotted stag
rows.headWhy: Specific. The branched sweeping antlers with a forward brow tine and three upright points per beam are unmistakable and could not be swapped onto anything else in the batch. The long tapering muzzle and long thin neck support the read. The weakness is that the antlers are doing all the work — remove them and the skull underneath is the same tan wedge used on the Cow and Coyote.
rows.defect: Two anatomy misses on an otherwise convincing render. (1) The ears are missing. The row lists large upright cupped ears as a mustRead; what is present is one dark brown blob crowded against the antler bases, with no cup, no interior and no second ear. On a deer the ears are big, mobile, and set out to the sides well below the antler pedicles — they should be clearly separate from the antler bases and read at a glance. (2) There is no tail at all — the rump ends in a bare curve. A white-tailed or red deer type needs at least a short tail with a pale underside against a paler rump patch. Secondary: the spotting is heavy, black and clumped into a saddle blotch over the shoulder and back rather than the fawn dapple of small pale ovals arranged in loose rows along the flank, and the legs are straight tubes with no hock angle in the hind limb — the hind leg should bend back at the hock and forward at the stifle, which is a large part of a deer's read.
rows.fix: Draw two large cupped ears anchored low and wide on the skull, below and outside the antler pedicles, angled out and slightly forward, each about the length of the face, with a visible pale inner cup and a darker rim so they separate from the antlers. Add a short tail at the rump with a white underside, sitting against a pale rump patch. Change the spot pattern to small pale ovals with soft edges laid in horizontal rows down the flank over an unbroken tan ground, and remove the dark shoulder saddle. Put a real hock angle in the hind legs so the rear limb zigzags rather than dropping straight.

rows.readsAs: A stubby tan armadillo with a duck's bill glued on — a toy platypus-armadillo hybrid, not a pangolin.
rows.headWhy: Distinct only by accident: it is the sole head in the batch with a wide flat spatulate bill and a big round eye set high and forward. Nobody would confuse it with the others — but the distinguishing feature is a duck bill, which is the wrong animal. A pangolin skull is a short smooth blunt cone that tapers to a tiny mouth, narrower than the neck, with a nearly invisible pinhole eye.
rows.defect: Two mustReads fail outright. (1) The tail is a thin upward-hooked stub about 15% of body length — the pangolin's defining feature is a thick muscular tail AS LONG AS THE BODY, held low and tapering. What is drawn is a pig's curl. (2) The scales read as flat painted vertical chevrons/triangles airbrushed onto a smooth hide; there is no overlap, no raised edge, no pinecone stagger. Additionally the head has a flat duck bill instead of a conical snout, and the legs are four identical stubby posts with no sign of the huge digging foreclaws.
rows.fix: Replace the curled stub with a low, ground-trailing tail rooted at full torso width and tapering over a length equal to or greater than the torso, scaled on both faces. Rebuild the coat as discrete overlapping lamellae: rows of rounded-diamond plates whose lower edge casts a hard drop-shadow onto the plate beneath, staggered brick-fashion and shrinking toward the tail tip — an actual repeating element, not a gradient stripe. Cut the bill back to a short smooth cone with no mouth line and shrink the eye to a dark bead. Give the forelimbs oversized curved digging claws so it knuckle-walks on the wrists.

rows.readsAs: A shaggy grey capybara, or a scruffy young goat with a pig's nose.
rows.headWhy: Generic. Take the pink nostril disc, rounded muzzle and small dark eye off this head and put it on the Pig and nothing about the silhouette changes — the two heads are the same geometry in two colours. Nothing here says peccary specifically.
rows.defect: The signature mustRead is entirely missing: there are NO tusks. The mouth is a single thin drawn line with nothing projecting from it, so the one feature that separates a peccary from a pig is absent. Secondary: the bristle strokes are stuck to the outer silhouette edge as a fringe of loose hairs and do not read as a coat lying on the body — the interior stays smooth and flat. The ears are near-invisible dark nubs.
rows.fix: Add two short, straight, dagger-like tusks emerging from the upper jaw and pointing STRAIGHT DOWN past the lower lip — pale ivory against the dark mouth line so they read at thumbnail size, and explicitly not curled up like a boar's. Then re-differentiate the skull from the Pig's: peccary has a wedge-shaped head, flatter cheek, straighter dorsal profile from crown to snout, and the snout disc should be smaller and grey-brown rather than a big pink pig disc. Bring the bristles inboard as a raised dorsal crest along the spine instead of an edge fringe.

rows.readsAs: A pink capybara or a hairless piglet — the snout says pig, the proportions do not.
rows.headWhy: Generic. The pink nostril disc is the only identifier and the Peccary has the same one. Swap the two heads and the only tell is hue. The dark shape on the crown reads as a stuck-on fringe of hair, not as an ear — it sits on top of the skull rather than hinging from its side, so the pig's big forward-flopping ear leaf never registers.
rows.defect: Two of the three mustReads fail. (1) There is NO tail at all — the corkscrew curl, which is the pig's second-most recognizable feature after the snout, simply is not drawn; the rump ends in a plain grey shading blob. (2) The legs are medium-length slim posts, so the body sits high and the animal reads leggy; a pig is a deep barrel slung LOW on very short thick legs. The dark crown shape also fails to read as an ear.
rows.fix: Draw the tail: a short tight corkscrew of two to three coils springing horizontally off the top of the rump, kept in silhouette against the background so it reads at small size. Shorten the legs by roughly a third and thicken them, dropping the belly line to about a leg's-width above the ground so the barrel dominates. Move the ear off the crown to the side of the skull and make it a large triangular leaf flopping forward over the eye. Widen the snout disc and square off the muzzle so it is visibly blunter than the Peccary's wedge.

rows.readsAs: A white goat, or a small white pony — nothing in this picture reads as a bear.
rows.headWhy: Generic. Narrow pale muzzle, small round ear, dark bead eye — the identical description fits the Possum in this same batch, and swapping those two heads would pass unnoticed. The one bear-specific cue that exists, a slight Roman convexity over the nose, is too subtle to survive at thumbnail size, and the grey disc behind the ear reads as a smudge.
rows.defect: The limbs are the batch's generic thin tube legs ending in small dark HOOF-like tips. The mustRead calls for huge furred paws and there is no paw mass anywhere — this is the single worst error in the image, because slender hooved legs make it an ungulate. The body is also wrong for the reference: it is a short compact barrel rather than a long body with sloping shoulders, and the neck is short and thick rather than long, so the polar-bear-specific proportions are inverted.
rows.fix: Replace the hooved tubes with massive plantigrade paws — the whole sole flat on the ground, paw width at least equal to limb thickness, a shaggy fur skirt overhanging the foot, and short dark claw tips. Thicken the forelimbs into columns. Then lengthen the torso by roughly 25% and run the topline as a long shallow slope descending from the haunch forward to the shoulder with NO hump, and extend the neck so the small head carries well forward and low of the shoulder line — that low-slung long neck is the polar bear's read and it is what currently distinguishes nothing.

rows.readsAs: A small cream-coloured goat or a pale short-haired dog.
rows.headWhy: Generic. Pale narrow muzzle plus a small dark ear nub — the same head as the Polar Bear in this batch with a darker ear. None of the opossum's identifiers are present: no bare pink nose tip, no dark eye ringed by the white face mask, and the ears are opaque dark triangles rather than the large, thin, naked black-and-pink leaves that stick out clear of the skull.
rows.defect: All three mustReads fail. (1) The tail is a short FURRED hook curled up over the rump — the Virginia opossum's tail must be long, naked, pale and scaly, roughly body length, trailing low. This drawing has the Australian possum's tail, which the batch note explicitly rules out. (2) The coat is a smooth flat cream with no grizzling and no shag — it should be a coarse two-tone salt-and-pepper grey with a ragged outline. (3) The feet are plain tubes; the opossum has five-toed hand-like feet with an opposable hind thumb, which is a marsupial giveaway.
rows.fix: Rebuild the tail as a long bare rat tail, thick and pale at the base and tapering to a point, drawn with fine ring-scale banding, hanging low behind rather than curling up. Regrizzle the coat by layering dark guard hairs over a pale underfur and let them break the silhouette so the outline is ragged. Give the face a white mask against a dark crown, a small pink nose button, and swap the ear nubs for large thin bare ear leaves — dark at the base fading to pink at the rim — held out from the head. Open the toes into five splayed digits.

rows.readsAs: A young tan deer with velvet antlers — a whitetail, not a pronghorn.
rows.headWhy: Specific, by headgear alone: it is the only horned/antlered head in the batch, so it could not be swapped without notice. But the specificity comes from an accessory rather than the skull. The skull itself — long tan muzzle, forward-set high eye — would read as generic ungulate if the headgear were removed, and it is currently the WRONG headgear.
rows.defect: The horns are drawn as pale, upright, multi-tined branching antlers — a deer's rack. A pronghorn carries black, laterally flattened horns that rise then HOOK SHARPLY FORWARD at the tip, with exactly ONE short prong jutting forward from the front edge roughly halfway up. Two more mustReads are also missing: there are no white throat bands and no white rump patch, so the animal's whole colour signature is absent and it renders as a flat monochrome tan.
rows.fix: Replace the antlers with two black horns: a thickened base, a smooth rise, a single short forward-pointing prong at mid-height, and a distinct backward-then-forward hook at the tip. Keep them dark so they silhouette. Then paint the markings — two crisp horizontal white bars across the throat under the jaw, a white belly and lower flank with a hard boundary against the tan, and a large white rump patch wrapping the tail base. Those three white shapes are what makes a pronghorn recognizable at any distance and none exist right now.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat or an appaloosa-marked dog — the pattern reads as ink splatter on a pale hide.
rows.headWhy: Generic. A dark-brown rounded muzzle with a small pale eye and a small rounded ear; strip the body away and it could sit on the Peccary or the Possum without anyone flagging it. The quoll's actual head cues — a sharply tapered pointed snout ending in a bare pink nose, and large eyes set far forward on a narrow dasyurid skull — are absent.
rows.defect: The spot polarity is inverted: this is a tan coat carrying BLACK blotches, whereas a quoll is a dark coat carrying WHITE spots. As drawn it reads leopard/appaloosa. The spots are also irregular splatter shapes rather than crisp discs. The batch's specific note fails too: the tail is a short pale brush with no spots on it, when the point of the species is that the white spots CONTINUE onto the tail. Finally the posture is wrong — long straight tube legs hold the body high and square, where a quoll is a low, long, slinking animal with the belly close to the ground.
rows.fix: Invert the pattern: dark chocolate-brown base coat with crisp round white spots of varying size scattered over the back and flanks, and continue those same white spots along the full length of the tail — that continuation is the identifying trait and must be visible. Lengthen the tail to roughly body length and keep it bushy but not brush-tipped. Shorten and bend the legs so the topline drops and the body runs low and horizontal in a stalking crouch. Sharpen the head to a narrow taper ending in a pink nose, and enlarge the eyes forward on the skull.

rows.readsAs: A generic tan deer or antelope with a bare, ear-less head
rows.headWhy: The lyre horns and the white throat/muzzle blaze do carry it — swap this head onto the Jackal and you would notice. But the horns are doing 100% of the work: the skull underneath is the same tapering wedge as the Jackal and Kudu, the horns are smooth tubes with no annular rings, and the head has NO EARS AT ALL. The 'per-family ear shape' pass did not reach this render.
rows.defect: (1) Both ears are entirely absent — the horns emerge from a bald skull. (2) No black rump/tail stripes; the rump is a plain tan lozenge with a dark shoulder blotch instead. (3) Horns lack the ~20 transverse rings that define an impala horn, and their spread is too narrow/too short for a lyre. (4) Legs are uniform thick columns with no black hock tuft and no visible cleft in the hoof — the mustRead 'extremely fine legs' is not met; they are the same limb the Kudu and Jackal have.
rows.fix: Add the missing ear: a narrow pointed leaf ~0.5x horn length, angled back-and-out, set BELOW and behind the horn base with a dark inner-ear channel. Ring the horns with 18-22 raised transverse bands that fade toward the smooth tip, and widen the lyre so the tips splay outward past the ear line before curving up. Thin the leg columns ~30% below the knee, taper them, split the hoof into two cloven halves, and paint a hard black brush tuft on the rear of the hind fetlock. Replace the shoulder blotch with the actual field mark: white rump panel bordered by three vertical black stripes (one down each thigh, one down the tail).

rows.readsAs: A tan horse foal or small donkey
rows.headWhy: Long blunt muzzle, tiny dark triangular ears, one large white-ringed eye set high — this is the same head as the Impala with the horns removed, and it would pass unnoticed on the Kinkajou or Kudu. Nothing canid is present: no stop between forehead and muzzle, no black nose pad, no cheek ruff, and the ears are small nubs rather than the 'large pointed erect ears' that are the single most recognizable jackal feature.
rows.defect: The whole animal is built on the ungulate chassis, not a canid one. Feet are dark blunt hoof blocks with no toes, pads or claws. The neck is long and arched and rises from a high withers exactly like a horse's. The tail is a stiff upward-sweeping bristle brush attached at croup height — a horse tail, not a low-carried bushy canid tail with a dark tip. Legs are straight columns with no hock angle, so there is no digitigrade rear geometry at all.
rows.fix: Swap to the paw/digitigrade limb: shorten the metacarpals, break the hind leg with a sharp hock angle, and terminate every foot in four visible toe pads plus a heel pad. Drop the tail attachment to below the hip line, make it a thick tapering bush carried low with a black distal third. Shorten the neck by ~35% and level it so the head is carried forward, not upright. Enlarge the ears to roughly 0.6x head length, erect, sharply triangular, with a pale inner cup and visible fur fringe. Add a canid stop and a black nose pad at the muzzle tip.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat or a hyena-headed calf
rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Leopard in this same batch — identical skull, identical single oversized forward-staring eye with a pale iris ring, identical large round dark ear disc planted flat on the top of the skull like a lemur's. There is no jaguar cranium here: no massive squared jaw, no wide zygomatic flare, no short deep muzzle. The head is also far too small for the body it sits on.
rows.defect: Feet are blunt dark hoof stubs, not paws — a big cat rendered on hooves. The tail is a thin cow-like whip carried upright and curled, instead of a heavy low-slung counterweight. The coat pattern is scattered irregular black blobs and clusters, not rosettes; a few read as broken rings but none contain the central spot that is the whole point of the note. Body is stocky but bulges at the belly rather than at the shoulder and haunch, so it reads bovine rather than muscular.
rows.fix: Rebuild the head at ~1.3x current scale on a jaguar skull: deep blocky jaw, broad cheeks wider than the braincase, short muzzle, and move the ear to a SMALL rounded cup set at the outer rear corner of the skull, not a disc on the crown. Give both eyes a round pupil set forward on the face. Replace hooves with broad soft paws — four toes, no claws showing. Thicken the tail to ~1.5x and let it hang in a low S. Redraw the pattern as discrete rosettes: a broken ring of 4-6 dark arcs, each ring enclosing one or two solid centre dots, larger and sparser over the flank, solid spots only on the head and lower legs.

rows.readsAs: A cream-coloured mongoose or a young otter
rows.headWhy: A pointed tapering snout with a small dark eye and a flat round dark ear patch — the same generic carnivoran wedge as the Jackal, and swapping the two would not be noticed. The mustRead calls for a round teddy-bear face with huge dark eyes; the render has a long snout and a small eye, which is the opposite silhouette. No short domed cranium, no broad forehead, no forward-set eyes.
rows.defect: Feet are blunt hoof-like stubs on an animal defined by grasping hands — no digits at all. The tail reads as a stiff crescent club of even thickness laid against the flank; it is neither thick at the base nor tapered nor curling, so nothing about it says prehensile. Body is a plain barrel with no arboreal crouch — a kinkajou should sit low with limbs bent under it, not stand tall on straight columns. Coat is uniform pale cream, not golden-brown.
rows.fix: Round the skull: dome the forehead, cut the snout to about one third its length, and enlarge both eyes to full round dark spheres set forward and close together. Keep the ears small and round but move them to the sides of the dome. Replace the stub feet with five-toed grasping hands, toes splayed and curling. Rebuild the tail thick at the root, tapering steadily over ~1.2x body length, and curl the last third into a full loop so the prehensility reads. Lower the body on bent limbs, and warm the coat to golden-brown with a darker dorsal line.

rows.readsAs: A koala clinging to a tree — correctly and immediately
rows.headWhy: Easily the strongest head in the batch and not swappable with anything: front-facing round skull, two huge round fringed ears flanking it at cheek height, an enormous leathery spoon nose dominating the lower face, and small beady close-set eyes. Every mustRead facial feature is present and the proportions are right.
rows.defect: Two things, one anatomical. (1) ANATOMY: the forelimbs read only as two pale diagonal smudges overlapping the trunk — there are no hands, no digits, no opposable two-and-three grip on the bark, so the animal appears stuck to the trunk rather than gripping it, and the hind limbs are not resolvable at all. (2) SURFACE: the fur is drawn as long straight white needles radiating from the silhouette, which reads as static electricity or a burr rather than dense woolly pelage, and the body fill under them is a flat mauve gradient with no fur texture inside the outline.
rows.fix: Draw both forepaws wrapping the trunk edges with visible digits — two thumbs opposed against three fingers — and dark curved claws biting the bark; add one hind foot braced lower on the trunk. For the coat, shorten the radiating hairs to about a third their length, vary their length and angle so the rim breaks up irregularly instead of spiking uniformly, tint them the body grey rather than white, and carry short directional fur strokes INTO the body fill so the interior is not bare gradient. Shift the body hue from mauve toward warm ash-grey with a white chest bib.

rows.readsAs: An antelope that has been scribbled on with a black marker
rows.headWhy: The tall corkscrew horns are unmistakable and no other head in the batch could stand in for it. But that is again the horns alone — the skull below is the same tapering wedge shared with the Impala and Jackal, the enormous rounded satellite-dish ears are simply not there (there is only a small dark ring beside the eye), and the face is crossed by black scribbles where the white chevron should be.
rows.defect: (1) The flank stripes are rendered as dense ragged BLACK brush scribbles that mass into a single dark blot over the shoulder and back, and they run diagonally as well as vertically. The mustRead is 6-10 thin WHITE vertical stripes; the render inverts the value and destroys the count. The same scribbles spill onto the neck and face. (2) The signature ears are missing. (3) The tail is a brown lollipop — a thin stalk ending in an oval club — floating clear of the rump. (4) Horn spirals are shallow, only about 1.5 turns, and read as smooth ribbons rather than keeled.
rows.fix: Repaint the stripes as 8 clean thin WHITE vertical lines, evenly spaced from behind the shoulder to the haunch, each following the barrel's curve and stopping short of the belly; clear all scribble off the neck and face and replace it with a single white chevron between the eyes. Add the ears: two very large rounded fans, wider than the skull, set low and outward at the horn base, with pale inner cups. Rebuild the tail as a tapering fringed brush attached flush to the rump, dark above, white beneath. Deepen the horn spiral to 2.5 turns and add the raised spiral keel ridge so it reads as bone, not tube.

rows.readsAs: The same spotted goat as the Jaguar, slightly leaner
rows.headWhy: This is the clearest failure of the standing complaint in the batch: the head is the Jaguar's head. Same undersized skull, same flat round ear disc on the crown, same single big pale-ringed eye, same short muzzle stub. The two files could be swapped and nobody would know which was which. Neither carries a cat skull at all.
rows.defect: Feet are dark hoof stubs — no paws, no toes. The tail is a short thin upcurled whip roughly a third of body length, when the mustRead requires a thick tail nearly as long as the body; the Jaguar's tail is the same part. The body is not low-slung: it stands tall on straight vertical columns with a level back and no shoulder-blade rise, so the predatory crouch is absent. The rosettes are closer to correct than the Jaguar's but many are still solid blobs, and some do contain centre dots, which is exactly backwards from the note.
rows.fix: Differentiate the head from the Jaguar at the skull level: narrower braincase, longer and more delicate muzzle, smaller cheeks, and move the ear to a small rounded cup on the outer rear of the skull with a black backing and white ocellus. Give a round pupil in a golden iris on both eyes. Replace hooves with soft paws showing four toe pads. Lengthen and thicken the tail to ~0.9x body length, hanging low with an upward hook only at the tip, and band its distal half. Lower the chest and shorten the legs so the belly line sits closer to the elbow. Clean the pattern to true HOLLOW rings — 4-6 dark arcs around a bare coat-coloured centre with no dot — reserving solid spots for the head, throat and lower limbs.

rows.readsAs: a grey hornless sheep or lamb standing side-on — a barrel body on four thin sticks with a dark face mask
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is the exact same rounded wedge skull as Brown Bear — same brow dome, same small round dark ear at the top-rear, same white-ringed eye, same short tapered snout with a button nose — recoloured dark grey. Swap the two heads and only the hue changes. Nothing bear-specific: no long straight facial profile, no tan muzzle, no low-set forward-facing ear pair.
rows.defect: This is not a bear body plan at all — it is the shared bovid rig. The four legs are equal-length thin tubes ending in small dark POINTED hoof tips with a fetlock band; a bear must land on broad plantigrade soles with the whole rear foot on the ground and short curved claws showing. The topline is flat-to-slightly-shoulder-high, so the mustRead 'rump higher than shoulders' is inverted — the hindquarters read LOWER than the front. Coat is mid-grey, not black, and the muzzle is the same grey-black as the mask rather than tan, so the one colour cue that separates a black bear from every other bear is absent. Two round bulges hang under the belly line (the shared haunch/udder blobs) that no bear has.
rows.fix: Give the ursine family its own limb+foot: shorten and thicken the legs, drop the hock so the hind limb is angled not straight, and terminate every foot in a wide flat sole polygon with 4-5 short curved claw nubs at the toe edge — no fetlock band, no hoof point. Rotate the pelvis up so the sacrum sits ~8% of body height above the withers and let the neck attach LOW so the head carries below the rump. Recolour the coat to near-black with a warm tan wedge covering the muzzle from the nose to below the eye, and delete the two under-belly bulges from the bear torso solid.

rows.readsAs: a spotted fawn or young deer with dark tufty ears
rows.headWhy: Specific, but only barely and only by two decals: it is the only head in the batch with pointed ears carrying black tufts, and the only one with a yellow-green iris and a VERTICAL slit pupil. Both read clearly. Underneath them the skull is still the shared tapered wedge with a dog-like projecting snout — a cat needs a short flat face where the nose sits almost between the eyes, plus the cheek ruff, and neither is there.
rows.defect: The body is a deer, not a cat. The legs are long straight ungulate columns ending in small dark HOOF tips — a bobcat must have shorter, thicker, bent-hocked legs on soft rounded paws with toe pads. The chest is shallow and the spine is a level deer topline instead of a cat's flexible shoulder-blade-high, low-slung carriage. The spot pattern is deer-fawn dappling (dense rosette-free blotches over the barrel) rather than the bobcat's broken bars down the legs and flanks. The bobbed tail reads correctly as a stub, and the mustRead cheek ruff is entirely missing — the jawline is bare.
rows.fix: Route this species to the feline limb type: shorten the legs by ~25%, add a visible carpal and a strongly angled hock, and replace the hoof tips with a three-lobed paw silhouette. Drop the chest and raise the scapula so the shoulder blades read above the spine. Shorten the muzzle hard — pull the nose back until it is under the eye line — and add the ruff as a fringed widening of the cheek/jaw outline below the ear, not as painted texture. Convert the flank spots to short horizontal bars on the forelegs and inner thighs.

rows.readsAs: a striped antelope — a kudu or bongo. The most legible animal in the batch.
rows.headWhy: Specific, but the specificity is carried entirely by the attached horns — tall, tightly twisted, close-set spirals that nothing else in the batch has. The skull under them is the same wedge as Bull and Buffalo. Real ears are missing altogether (the bongo's huge round leaf ears should be its second-loudest head feature), the eye is a plain white-ringed bead with no visible iris colour, and the mustRead white chevron between the eyes is absent.
rows.defect: Three anatomy/marking faults. (1) Stripe polarity is inverted: the flank carries DARK stripes painted over tan, and a solid dark saddle block sits across the back like a rug; the bongo's signature is thin WHITE stripes over a chestnut-red ground with no saddle. (2) No ears — the horn bases occupy the whole ear zone, so the head has nothing hanging beside it. (3) The stripes wrap onto the face and neck, which turns the head into a continuation of the pattern instead of a chestnut head with a clean white chevron. The horns are also too thin and too vertical: they should be heavy at the base and clearly backswept over the neck.
rows.fix: Invert the stripe pass — chestnut-red ground, 10-12 narrow near-white vertical stripes from spine to belly, delete the dark saddle and stop the stripe field at the shoulder so the neck and head stay clean. Add a pair of large rounded leaf ears set low and outward beneath the horn bases. Thicken the horn base ~60% and rake the whole horn back ~20 degrees so the tips sit over the withers. Paint a single white chevron across the bridge of the nose between the eyes.

rows.readsAs: a brown sheep, or a capybara with a lumpy back
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is pixel-for-pixel the Black Bear head in a warmer brown — same brow dome, same small round dark ear at top-rear, same white-ringed eye, same tapering snout and button nose. The mustRead dished concave face is not there: the profile from brow to nose is straight-to-convex. Swap it with Black Bear and no one would notice.
rows.defect: Bear anatomy is absent below the neck. The feet are small dark POINTED hoof tips with fetlock bands — the mustRead 'long straight pale digging claws' does not exist anywhere in the image. Legs are four equal thin tubes with no bend. The shoulder hump is present only as a soft rise in the coat gradient behind the neck; the tallest point of the animal is actually the mid-back blob, so the hump does not do its diagnostic job of making the FRONT the highest point. Two round bulges hang under the belly (the shared haunch/udder blobs) that read as an udder on a bear.
rows.fix: Same ursine limb routing as Black Bear: thick, short, hock-bent legs on broad flat plantigrade soles, then add 4-5 LONG straight pale claws projecting forward past the toe edge of the front feet (these should be visible at 440px — they are the single read). Build the hump as a genuine silhouette event: raise the withers contour ~12% above the sacrum so the topline slopes downhill from shoulder to rump. Concave the facial profile — dip the bridge of the nose below the line from brow to nose tip — and widen the forehead. Delete the under-belly bulges.

rows.readsAs: a grey ox or cow wearing a pale crescent like a moustache over its mouth
rows.headWhy: Generic. Strip the horns and this is the Bull head verbatim: same wedge skull, same dark topknot patch, same white-ringed bead eye, same blunt muzzle. The mustRead fused helmet boss across the forehead does not exist — the horns spring from two separate points. The mustRead large fringed drooping ears are missing entirely; there is nothing hanging beside the head.
rows.defect: The horns are malformed and mis-anchored: they emerge from the side of the face and curl DOWN and FORWARD across the muzzle so the crescent ends up floating over the mouth, reading as a moustache or a nose ring rather than as horn. They also read as flat ribbon with no taper to a point. Secondly, the mustRead 'massive shoulders' fails — the hindquarters are as bulky as the forequarters and the neck is a thin bridge, so the mass is even front-to-back instead of front-loaded.
rows.fix: Rebuild the horn as one unit: a broad ridged boss spanning the whole forehead between the eyes, with the horns exiting sideways from the boss edges, dropping below the eye line, then sweeping UP and back to points clear of the face — never crossing in front of the muzzle. Hang a large drooping fringed ear directly beneath each horn base. Rebalance the torso solid: add ~20% depth and height to the shoulder/withers region and thicken the neck to match, then taper the barrel toward a narrower rump.

rows.readsAs: a beige cow or ox — nothing about it says male or bull
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is the Buffalo head recoloured with the horns rotated upward, and the same wedge/brow/bead-eye/blunt-muzzle template that Bongo and Camel are also built on. A bull head needs a short broad blocky skull with a wide flat forehead, small eyes set wide, and a heavy square jaw; this one is a narrow tapering wedge.
rows.defect: Two of the three mustReads are simply absent. There is no dewlap — the underside of the neck is a clean straight line from jaw to chest where a heavy pendulous fold should hang. And the humped neck-and-shoulder mass is only a flat dark colour patch over the shoulder, not a shape: the neck is visibly thinner than the barrel and the topline is level, so the animal has no crest. The horns are also wrong-way: they arc up and back like an antelope's instead of short and forward-curving.
rows.fix: Add a real crest — a raised muscular mound on top of the neck just ahead of the withers, making the neck as deep as the ribcage, and let it be the highest point of the topline. Hang a dewlap as a scalloped, wavy-edged flap of skin from the jaw down along the throat to the brisket (this is the fastest bull read at thumbnail size). Shorten the horns to about one head-width, thicken the base, and curve the tips FORWARD past the eye line. Broaden and shorten the skull, widen the forehead between the horn bases, and square off the jaw.

rows.readsAs: a llama or a camel with a lump strapped to its back
rows.headWhy: Specific — the one genuinely distinct head in the batch. Domed forehead, long tapering muzzle with the lower lip dropping past the upper, tiny nub ears set far back, and the head carried at the top of a long arched neck. Nothing else here reads like it. Only weakness: the eye is the same white-ringed bead as the cattle and shows no heavy lash or hood, and the mustRead 'prominent eyes' is not delivered.
rows.defect: The hump is a pasted-on object, not part of the animal. It is a separate dome with a visible hard seam where it meets the back and a colour break, so it reads as cargo rather than as body. It is also competing with the two round under-belly bulges from the shared torso solid, which on a camel read as a second and third hump hanging beneath it — a camel's belly line should be shallow and tucked. The legs also fail the note: they are roughly 40% of total height and are straight untapered tubes ending in small dark POINTED hoof tips, where a camel needs very long legs with a knobbly stifle/knee and a broad soft two-toed pad that splays flat on the ground.
rows.fix: Merge the hump into the torso silhouette — build it as a single continuous back contour that rises from the withers, peaks over the mid-spine and falls to the croup, with no seam and no colour break — then delete the two under-belly bulges and tuck the belly up sharply behind the ribcage. Lengthen the legs by ~35% so leg mass is half the total height, add a visible knee bulge and callused elbow pads, and swap the hoof tip for a wide flat splayed two-toed pad. Add a heavy lashed upper lid to the eye.

rows.readsAs: a turned-wood weasel toy in pale beige with a chocolate head and a feather-duster tail
rows.headWhy: Identical construction to the Mongoose in this same batch: same rounded dome cranium, same single small round ear set at the crown, same short blunt muzzle, same oversized white-sclera eye with a black round pupil at the same relative position. Only the fill colour differs. Swap the two heads and nobody could tell.
rows.defect: Three anatomy failures. (1) Coat value is inverted — the row calls for glossy dark chocolate fur, and the body is rendered pale tan/beige with only the head dark, so the animal reads as two different animals joined at the neck; no white chin patch is present. (2) The tail is a thin frayed wisp of individual hair strokes with a white dot at the tip — it has no solid core, so it reads as a feather duster or a wick rather than the mink's thick furred tail. (3) The four legs terminate as blunt cut-off cylinders with no foot at all — no paw, no toes, no ankle taper. Additionally a hard specular seam runs the full length of the spine like a lathe highlight, reinforcing the wooden-dowel read.
rows.fix: Recolour the whole pelt to a dark saturated chocolate with a warm specular sheen and drop a small cream chin/throat patch under the jaw so the head stops reading as a separate piece. Rebuild the tail as a solid tapering cone about 40% of body length with fur strokes riding ON the silhouette rather than replacing it, and kill the white tip dot. Add real mustelid paws: a small five-toed pad wider than the leg shaft, planted flat, with a visible ankle narrowing above it. For the head, differentiate from Mongoose: mink skull is flatter and broader across the cheeks with a shorter muzzle and much lower-set, barely-emergent rounded ears half-buried in the pelt — pull the ear down and shrink it, widen the cheek, shorten the muzzle.

rows.readsAs: a pale ribbed grub, or a tiny dachshund with a duck's bill
rows.headWhy: Specific by absence — it is the only head in the batch with no external ear and no open eye, and it carries a long tapering snout that nothing else here has. But the specificity is accidental: the snout terminates in a flat dark-edged wedge that reads as a duck bill, and there is still a visible dark eye dot despite the spec calling for hidden eyes.
rows.defect: The single defining feature of a mole is missing: there are no spade forepaws. All four limbs are identical tiny pale nubs of the same size, set at normal quadruped stations well behind the head, when the forelimbs should be enormous outward-rotated shovels sitting almost beside the skull. Secondary failures: the snout is a flat grey wedge, not a pink fleshy point; the body carries hard horizontal corrugation lines that make it read as a segmented larva instead of a neckless velvet cylinder; and a dark eye dot is visible on a species specced eyes-hidden.
rows.fix: Replace the front limbs with a dedicated mole forefoot: a broad palm rotated to face outward/backward, wider than it is long, silhouetted well outside the body line, with 4-5 pale claw spikes fanning off the leading edge, and move the whole shoulder forward so the paw sits level with the cheek. Shrink the hindlimbs to short nubs by comparison. Tip the snout with a pink fleshy point and add pink to the nose pad. Remove the eye dot entirely and replace the corrugated body lines with a soft short-nap velvet shading that runs perpendicular to the body axis, no hard rings.

rows.readsAs: the same wooden weasel toy as the Mink, in cream instead of tan
rows.headWhy: This is the Mink head with a lighter fill. Same dome cranium, same crown-mounted round ear, same blunt muzzle length, same big white-sclera eye. There is nothing on it that says mongoose — the row calls for a pointed tapering snout and the render gives a short blunt one.
rows.defect: Near-total duplication of the Mink render — identical torso solid, identical leg cylinders, identical frayed-wisp tail with the white tip dot, identical head. Beyond the duplication: the snout is blunt where it must taper to a point; the tail is a thin fraying brush instead of a thick tail tapering to a point, and it is the same tail asset as the Mink's; the legs again end in cut cylinders with no foot; and the torso carries the same lathe-highlight seam down the spine.
rows.fix: Force divergence from Mink at the skull: extend and taper the mongoose muzzle to a narrow point, flatten the cranium, set the small round ears low and to the SIDE of the head rather than on the crown, and give it a small dark round eye set forward near the snout base rather than the large centred eye. Rebuild the tail as a thick solid cone that starts as wide as the hips and tapers to a fine point, with a slightly bushy but silhouette-respecting fur edge. Add small digitigrade paws with visible non-retractile claws. Warm the coat to a grizzled grey with fine light/dark banding rather than flat cream.

rows.readsAs: a moose — correctly, though the antlers look like two cream ping-pong paddles with combs taped to the sides of its head
rows.headWhy: Unmistakable: palmate antlers, a long overhanging muzzle that droops well past the lower jaw, and a small eye set high and far back. No other head in the batch could stand in for it.
rows.defect: Three anatomy problems. (1) The antlers are flat 2D cream lozenges with straight comb tines, oriented in the picture plane and pasted directly onto the side of the skull with no visible pedicle or burr — they float in front of the face and one of them crosses over the eye region. There is no palm curvature and no perspective difference between the near and far antler. (2) The bell/dewlap is drawn as a thin white unfilled ellipse hanging at the throat, which reads as a hoop earring or a rope loop rather than a mass of hanging skin and hair. (3) A dark filled circle sits on the rump where the hip should be, reading as a knothole punched through the body rather than the head of the femur. Legs are correctly long but end in soft rounded stubs with no cloven split.
rows.fix: Model the antlers as solids: a short pedicle and burr rising from the skull above the eye, the near antler swept forward and foreshortened, the far antler smaller and partly occluded by the head; give each palm a convex curve with tines emerging from the palm's outer margin at varying lengths, and shade the palm's underside so it has thickness. Move both antlers behind and above the eye so nothing overlaps the face. Redraw the bell as a filled hanging lobe of dark hair with a soft ragged lower edge, attached along the throat line, not a closed outline. Replace the dark hip circle with a soft value shift for the haunch mass. Split the hoof tips into two cleats.

rows.readsAs: a white shaggy goat, correctly — but with scribbles for fur
rows.headWhy: Distinguished by the pair of short backswept horns rising directly above the eye plus the narrow tapering white muzzle. Nothing else in the batch carries that combination, so it would not swap.
rows.defect: (1) The horns are cream/tan, not the black dagger horns the species requires, so they blend into the white coat and lose all read at a glance. (2) The legs are perfectly smooth white tubes from body to hoof — the pantaloons, the single most named leg feature for this animal, are entirely absent. (3) The shaggy coat is rendered as loose white and grey scratch strokes that break the silhouette in every direction and trail a dirty grey halo behind the shoulder and rump, so the coat reads as scribble noise rather than long hanging hair; the strokes point outward radially instead of hanging with gravity. (4) A grey filled circle sits on the hip, the same knothole artifact as elsewhere in the batch. (5) The beard is barely present — only a small point under the chin.
rows.fix: Recolour the horns to matte black and give them a slight backward curve with visible ridging near the base. Add pantaloons: thicken the upper foreleg and thigh with a hanging skirt of hair whose lower edge is a clean ragged horizontal, ending abruptly above the ankle so the lower leg reads thin below it. Redirect all coat strokes to hang DOWNWARD from the topline and cluster the long hair at the shoulder hump, brisket and haunch instead of scattering evenly; clamp stroke length so the fur reads as a fringe on the silhouette rather than a halo, and delete the grey ghost strokes behind the body. Replace the hip circle with soft haunch shading. Lengthen the chin beard into a clear hanging wedge.

rows.readsAs: a grey pig or a large capybara
rows.headWhy: Unique within the batch by virtue of the big pink terminal nose disc on a long blunt head — but it is unique in the wrong direction: it reads as a domestic pig's snout disc, not a tapir's short flexible prehensile proboscis, and the huge white googly eye contradicts the small-eye spec.
rows.defect: (1) The snout terminates in a flat forward-facing pink disc with a single dark nostril hole, which is pig anatomy. A tapir's proboscis is a short mobile trunk that hangs DOWN over the mouth, overhanging the lower lip, with nostrils on its underside. (2) The eye is a large white almond with a dark iris — far too big for a species specced small eyes, and it makes the head cartoonish. (3) A solid black triangular wedge sits below and behind the nose, reading as an open wound or a gash rather than a mouth line; the white-rimmed lips the row calls for are not present. (4) The legs are thin smooth sticks with no visible toes, on an animal whose limbs are stout columns with three visible toes behind and four in front. (5) The same dark filled hip circle appears on the rump. (6) The woolly coat is a sparse layer of grey scratch strokes over an otherwise smooth grey body, so it still reads as bare hide with hairs stuck on.
rows.fix: Rebuild the snout as a downward-drooping flexible proboscis: taper the muzzle then curl the last third down past the mouth line, nostrils on the underside, and give it a soft mobile silhouette rather than a hard disc. Shrink the eye to a small dark bead with a thin lid and set it further back, roughly midway along the skull. Replace the black wedge with a thin closed mouth line and add a clean pale cream rim along the upper and lower lip edges. Thicken the limbs into short columns and add distinct toe pads at the ground line. Replace the hip circle with soft shading. For the wool, thicken the coat into overlapping clumped locks that alter the body silhouette along the back and flanks so it reads long-haired, not stubbled.

rows.readsAs: a shaggy brown ram wearing a large cream hoop over its cheek
rows.headWhy: Distinct within the batch because of the large cream horn curl and the very low-carried head — but the horn geometry is bighorn-sheep, not musk ox, so the specificity is a misidentification rather than a win.
rows.defect: (1) The horn is drawn as a single near-closed cream ring lying flat against the side of the face, crossing the eye and cheek. The musk ox horn must originate from a broad helmet-like boss meeting its partner across the top of the forehead, then sweep DOWN past the cheek and hook OUT and UP away from the head — a shallow J in three dimensions, not a flat circle. The frontal boss is entirely missing, so the forehead is bare. (2) The hair curtain is a fringe of straight straw-coloured bristles that stop at mid-belly, leaving all four legs bare smooth tubes below; the defining feature is a skirt of guard hair hanging almost to the hooves. The bristles also read as broom straw because they are individually separated, uniformly straight and lighter than the body. (3) The same dark filled circle marks the hip. (4) Hooves are rounded stubs with no cleft.
rows.fix: Rebuild the horns: add a wide pale keratin boss spanning the forehead between the eyes, drop each horn from the boss's outer corner straight down along the cheek to below the jawline, then hook the tip outward and slightly upward and forward; keep the near horn clear of the eye. Extend the hair curtain down to just above the hooves as a continuous massed skirt with a ragged uneven hem, drawn as overlapping clumps in the body's own dark brown with only a few lighter guard hairs catching light — not as separated pale straws. Keep the pale saddle patch over the shoulders for contrast. Replace the hip circle with soft haunch shading and split the hoof tips into two cleats.

rows.readsAs: A small sandy pony or donkey foal with a bottle-brush tail — nobody would say 'wild dog'.
rows.headWhy: This head is byte-for-byte interchangeable with the Dog in the same batch: identical long horse wedge, identical blunt down-turned muzzle with a dark nose dot, identical small dark rounded ear pair, identical oversized white-sclera cartoon eye set high on the skull. Nothing canid is present — no domed cranium stepping down to a shorter muzzle, no stop, no cheek. The 'erect pointed triangular ear' the row demands is not there; the ears are small dark rounded nubs.
rows.defect: Wrong body plan entirely. (a) The four limbs are straight ungulate sticks ending in dark HOOF caps — a dingo needs digitigrade paws with four toes and a pad, and the row's white feet are absent. (b) The head/neck is a horse wedge, not a canid skull. (c) The tail is a radial spray of stiff dark bristles that reads as a scrub brush or porcupine fan, not a bushy straight canid tail. (d) Two pale elliptical discs are pasted on the belly/flank that correspond to no muscle group. (e) The body has no chest depth or tuck — a dingo is deep-chested with a waisted loin.
rows.fix: Route Dingo to the canid limb/foot type: digitigrade leg with a visible hock angle on the hind, ending in a compact four-toe paw with a white sock over the last 20% of the leg. Swap the skull to the canid profile — domed braincase, defined stop, muzzle ~40% of head length tapering to a black nose — and set erect pointed triangular ears with the ear opening facing forward. Rebuild the tail as a single tapered mass with fur silhouette breaking the outline, not a radial bristle fan. Delete the two flank discs and get the haunch mass from the torso solid's shading instead.

rows.readsAs: The same tan pony as the Dingo, one shade more orange.
rows.headWhy: Completely generic and duplicated — swap it with the Dingo head and no one on earth could tell which was which. Same wedge skull, same blunt muzzle, same tiny dark rounded ears, same big round white eye in the same position. The row asks for 'a muzzle ending in a black nose' and 'erect or folded ears'; the render gives a horse's muzzle and two dark nubs. Nothing distinguishes a dog from a dingo here, and nothing distinguishes either from an equid.
rows.defect: Same wrong body plan as the Dingo: hoofed stick legs on a canid, ungulate wedge head, and a bristle-fan tail. The tail is additionally wrong for the row — it must be a plumed tail carried ABOVE the back line; here it hangs at or below croup height as a spiky fan. Torso is a smooth barrel with no ribcage/loin transition and carries the same two pasted-on pale flank discs. Because Dingo and Dog resolve to near-identical images, the pair fails as a set even before either fails on its own.
rows.fix: Give both canids the paw foot type and canid skull, then deliberately separate them: the Dog should read heavier and shorter-muzzled with a broader chest, a folded (drop) ear, and a plumed tail carried in an upward arc above the topline; the Dingo stays lean, longer-muzzled, prick-eared, tail straight and low. Even a 15% difference in muzzle length and leg-to-body ratio will break the twinning.

rows.readsAs: A pale grey pony with oddly round ears — 'donkey' is a reasonable guess, which makes this the most successful read in the batch.
rows.headWhy: The only species cue is the pair of dark ears, and they are bolted onto the exact same blank used for the Camel and Eland — same long tapering wedge, same faint smile-curve mouth line, same big round eye with white sclera and a dot pupil at the same height. Mask the ears and the head is unidentifiable. The ears themselves are also wrong shape: short, wide and rounded like a koala's, when the row's diagnostic feature is a VERY LONG upright ear roughly the length of the face.
rows.defect: (a) Ears far too short and too round for a donkey — they should be roughly 0.8x face length, narrow, upright and leaf-shaped with a dark rim and pale inner. (b) The short upright bristly mane is entirely missing; the crest is a bare smooth curve, which is exactly the cue that separates a donkey read from a generic pony read. (c) Two pale elliptical discs float on the barrel and haunch as pasted-on highlights unattached to any muscle. (d) No dorsal stripe or shoulder cross, and the muzzle lacks the pale mealy ring donkeys are known for. Tail and hooves are correct — the cow-like tail tufted only at the tip is right, and the dark hoof caps are right.
rows.fix: Lengthen and narrow the ears to a true leaf and give them the dark tip/pale interior split. Add the short erect brush mane as a row of stiff hairs standing off the crest from poll to withers. Replace the two floating flank discs with shading driven by the torso solid so shoulder and haunch read as volume. Add the pale mealy muzzle ring and the dark dorsal stripe — cheap, and both push the read from 'pony' to 'donkey'.

rows.readsAs: A camel or llama — the hump carries the read, so the species does land, but the hump looks like a separate object resting on the animal's back.
rows.headWhy: The head is the shared batch wedge — same taper, same white-sclera round eye, same tiny dark ear, same mouth line — differing from the Eland only by the absence of horns and from the Donkey only by smaller ears. The one camel-specific gesture, the drooping lower lip, is a small notch at the muzzle tip and does not survive at thumbnail size. The heavy brow, the bulging eye set under a bony orbital ridge with long lashes, and the split upper lip are all absent.
rows.defect: (a) The hump is a detached pale dome sitting on top of the spine with its own outline and its own cast shadow — it reads as a bag, not as fat continuous with the back. Its base is narrower than the back it sits on, which is what creates the seam. (b) Feet are dark hoof caps on straight sticks; the row calls for splayed padded feet and knobbly knee pads, and camels are the one large ungulate whose broad two-toed pad is genuinely diagnostic. (c) The shoulders do not slope — the row wants the neck rising from sloped shoulders, but the topline in front of the hump is flat. (d) The neck is a uniform tube with no thickening at the base and no crest. (e) Same two pasted-on pale flank discs as the rest of the batch.
rows.fix: Make the hump part of the torso silhouette: widen its base to the full back width and blend the front and rear slopes into the withers and croup so there is no independent outline or shadow. Swap the foot to the camel pad type — broad, splayed, soft-edged, wider than the leg above it — and add the dark knee callosity on the forelegs. Slope the shoulder down and forward so the neck emerges from a wedge rather than from a flat plank, and thicken the neck base. Deepen the brow over the eye and lengthen the drooping lip so the head carries a cue at small size.

rows.readsAs: A small tan deer or fawn with an unexplained dark hole in its hindquarter.
rows.headWhy: Same shared wedge again, shrunk. The differentiator is a pair of pale horns, and they read as forward-curving banana crescents rather than the tiny backswept spikes that define a duiker. There is no forehead tuft — that tuft plus the horns is the whole diagnostic package for this animal, and half of it is missing. Put this head on the Eland at matching scale and the only tell would be horn size.
rows.defect: (a) A large near-black circular blob sits on the near haunch. It is much darker than any other shading on the body and reads as a hole, a wound, or a decal rather than muscle — this is the most damaging single element in the picture. (b) The horns curve FORWARD and up; duiker horns are short straight spikes angled BACKWARD in line with the face. (c) The forehead tuft is absent.
