(d) The diagnostic posture is missing: the row calls for a hunched arched back higher at the rump, but the topline here is nearly level with only a slight rise, so the crouching duiker gesture never registers. (e) Legs are uniform tapered sticks with no visible pastern or fetlock above the cloven foot.
rows.fix: Kill the black haunch disc — clamp haunch shading to the same value range as the shoulder so it reads as a rounded mass, not a spot. Rebuild the horns as two short straight spikes raked back at roughly the angle of the nose bridge, and add the reddish forehead tuft between them. Raise the croup above the withers by 8-12% of body height and drop the head so the back arches — that silhouette alone identifies a duiker. Add fetlock definition above the cloven hoof.

rows.readsAs: A pale kudu or impala — a slender antelope with long curled horns. Not an ox-sized animal.
rows.headWhy: The head is the Camel's head with horns added — identical wedge, identical mouth line, identical round white-sclera eye, identical dark ear nub. The horns are the only species signal, and they read as smooth lyre-shaped kudu curves with no visible spiral ridging, so even that cue is pointing at the wrong antelope. The eland's actual head cues — a short broad blocky muzzle and a heavy brow — are absent.
rows.defect: (a) The dewlap is missing entirely. The row names it and it is the single most recognizable eland feature; the throat here is a clean thin curve. (b) No shoulder hump — the topline is straight, and the whole animal carries impala-light mass on thin legs when an eland is the largest antelope alive, bull-necked and heavy-shouldered. (c) The horns are smooth open curves; eland horns are STRAIGHT and tightly spiralled with a visible keel ridge winding up them. (d) The pale flank discs recur here as two soft ellipses that flatten the barrel rather than describing rib and haunch. (e) Legs are too long and too fine for the body they carry.
rows.fix: Add a deep loose dewlap hanging from the jaw to the brisket with its own sagging outline — this alone fixes most of the read. Build a shoulder hump above the withers and thicken the neck and forequarter so mass sits forward; shorten and thicken the legs by ~15%. Replace the curved horns with a near-straight backswept pair carrying a visible helical ridge. Broaden and blunt the muzzle so the head reads bovine rather than gazelle.

rows.readsAs: A grey elephant wearing a saddle blanket — the trunk and tusks sell the species instantly, but a large dark grey slab is stuck to the middle of its ribcage.
rows.headWhy: Genuinely specific and impossible to confuse with anything else in the batch: a ground-reaching trunk, two curved white tusks, and a domed cranium. No other head here has an appendage of any kind. That said, the eye is the same oversized white-sclera cartoon eye used on every other animal in this batch, which is badly wrong for an elephant — the row asks for a SMALL eye, and elephants have tiny eyes buried in wrinkled lids. The eye is the one part of this head that got copy-pasted.
rows.defect: (a) THE EAR IS OFF THE HEAD. The large dark fan sits over the shoulder and ribcage, centred well behind the jaw, overlapping the torso like a blanket, and its leading edge cuts across the body with a hard machined arc. An elephant's ear must attach directly behind the eye on the skull. There is also a second smaller grey plate sitting on top of the cranium doing nothing. (b) The trunk appears to emerge from the cheek/jaw line rather than from between the eyes at the front of the face, and the head has no forehead-to-trunk continuity. (c) The trunk tip is a blunt rounded stub — the row's two grasping lips are absent — and the trunk is banded with regular horizontal stripes that read as a printed pattern, not as skin rings. (d) The back is not dipped; the topline rises to a lump behind the head and then runs flat, so the saddle-back cue is missing. (e) The legs, especially the hind pair, are too slender and too far apart to read as pillars supporting that mass. Feet and toenails are correct.
rows.fix: Reattach the ear: anchor its top edge to the skull immediately behind and above the eye, and let it hang down and back so its trailing edge just reaches the shoulder — never crossing the ribcage. Remove the redundant plate on top of the cranium. Move the trunk root to the front of the face between the eyes and blend forehead into trunk as one continuous mass; taper the last 15% and split the tip into two small opposed lips. Replace the even stripe banding with irregular rings that follow the trunk's curve and compress on the inside of the bend. Shrink the eye to roughly a third of its current size and sink it under a heavy lid. Dip the spine behind the shoulder and thicken all four legs into true columns.

rows.readsAs: A stylized lion — the round mane and black tail tuft sell it immediately; closest wrong guess would be a plush lion toy
rows.headWhy: Specific, but the MANE is doing all the work, not the skull. The actual head is a tiny pale wedge with a black nose bud and a yellow slit-pupil eye poking out of a fur pom. Strip the mane and this muzzle is interchangeable with the Maned Wolf's. Worse, the ear is drawn as a flat brown DISC with a darker concentric ring sitting loose on the mane surface, well behind and above the eye — it reads as a coin, a monocle or a bullet wound stuck to the mane rather than an ear attached to a skull.
rows.defect: 1) The ear is a detached flat ringed disc floating on the mane silhouette, not a rounded ear rooted on the skull. 2) A second unexplained pale oval disc sits on the mid-torso over the shoulder, the same circular-patch artifact, reading as a bald spot. 3) The forelimb is a single thin tapered peg noticeably shorter and thinner than the hind limbs, and it hangs from a chest with no depth at all — a lion is front-heavy with a deep brisket and forelegs at least as thick as the hind. 4) Feet are small dark rounded caps that read closer to hooves than to padded cat paws — no toes, no pad.
rows.fix: Re-root the ear: draw it as a small rounded cup on the TOP-BACK of the skull dome, half-buried in mane fur with a few mane strands crossing its base, and kill the concentric ring (give it a darker inner concha wedge instead of a centered circle). Delete the torso oval or replace it with a soft directional shading gradient over the scapula. Rebuild the front end: drop the chest floor 10-12% lower than the belly line, thicken the foreleg to match or exceed the hind cannon, and terminate both in a paw with 3-4 visible toe lobes and a heel pad instead of a hoof cap.

rows.readsAs: A pale goat or a young alpaca — the S-neck says camelid but the head furniture says goat kid
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is a small cream dome with a pointed muzzle, one large dark eye and a dark clump on top — the same pale dome the Meerkat is wearing, and swapping the two would go unnoticed. The mustRead long banana-curved ears are absent: what is there is a short dark bristly tuft barely taller than the skull, which reads as a topknot or a pair of horn buds, not llama ears. A raised pale bump on the upper muzzle also reads as a wart/growth rather than a nostril.
rows.defect: 1) Ears are a stubby dark tuft, not the long inward-curving banana ears that are the single most identifying llama feature. 2) A hard-edged dark CIRCLE sits on the rear haunch — a flat disc artifact, not shading. 3) There is no shoulder: the neck springs vertically out of the top of the barrel with zero scapula mass or chest in front of the forelegs, so the head is cantilevered over empty space. 4) The torso reads as two overlapping spheres (a big rear balloon plus a smaller front one) with a visible seam between them rather than one solid barrel with a level back.
rows.fix: Replace the ear tuft with two long tapered leaf ears roughly 1.3x the skull height, curved inward toward each other so the tips nearly touch, with a pale inner face. Delete the rump circle; use an elongated soft gradient following the femur instead. Add a chest block forward of the forelegs and a wedge of shoulder mass where the neck meets the barrel so the neck rises from IN FRONT of the withers, not from the spine's midpoint. Merge the two torso spheres into a single hull with one continuous level topline.

rows.readsAs: A spotted fawn or a young sika deer — nobody would say cat
rows.headWhy: Generic and, worse, wrong family. Small narrow triangular head with a pointed deer muzzle, a plain dark rounded ear and a single yellow eye. The three mustReads that would make it a lynx head — the long black ear tufts, the flared cheek ruff, the short broad cat face — are all absent. This head could be dropped onto the Llama or the Maned Wolf and nobody would notice.
rows.defect: Nothing on this render is feline. No ear tufts at all (the ear is a plain rounded nub). No facial ruff — the cheeks are flat against the skull. Legs are thin deer cannons ending in small dark hoof-like caps, not the oversized snowshoe paws, and the hind legs are not longer than the front so the rump does not stand high. No tail is drawn anywhere — even a bobtail should read as a stub. The coat is scattered hard-edged blackish blobs like a fawn's dappling rather than a lynx's soft broken rosettes, and there is another flat dark DISC artifact on the haunch.
rows.fix: Rebuild as a cat: broaden and shorten the skull, drop the muzzle length by half, and add two black tufts at least 40% of ear height rising off the ear tips. Flare a ruff of downward-pointing fur from below the cheekbones to the jawline so the head silhouette widens below the eyes. Swap hooves for wide splayed paws drawn oversized (roughly 1.5x what the leg thickness implies) with visible toe lobes, and lengthen the hind limb so the hip sits above the shoulder. Add a 15-20% body-length stub tail with a black tip. Replace the blob dapples with softer, smaller broken rosettes and delete the haunch disc.

rows.readsAs: A cartoon fox-deer with Valentine ears — the huge dark ears and orange coat read fox, the stilty legs read deer
rows.headWhy: Distinctive within this batch — nothing else has the very long thin tapered snout plus that enormous dark ear mass — but the specificity is coming from a DEFECT: the two ears have merged into a single continuous dark brown heart shape with no gap, no separate left/right, and no inner concha. It reads as one heart-shaped hat rather than two erect ears. The eye is also a plain white almond with a dark dot, cartoon-flat, with no iris colour.
rows.defect: 1) Ears fused into one heart-shaped mass — no separation between them, no inner ear surface, no attachment point on the skull. 2) The black stockings are missing entirely: the legs are the same orange as the body with only faintly darker feet, which throws away half of what makes this animal recognizable. 3) The legs are long but not stilt-long — they are roughly 45% of standing height when the reference calls for ~60%; the barrel also has too much depth, so the animal reads chunky rather than small-bodied-on-poles. 4) The dark neck-and-shoulder mane is absent. 5) The tail is a straw-bristle broom attached high on the MID-BACK, projecting horizontally, with a pale blob at its end — it does not emerge from the rump and reads as a paintbrush stuck into the spine.
rows.fix: Split the ear mass into two clearly separate erect ears with a visible gap of at least one ear-width at the base, each with a pale inner concha and a defined root on the skull. Paint black from mid-forearm and mid-shin down to the toes on all four legs. Extend the limbs ~30% and shallow the barrel by ~20% so leg length dominates the silhouette. Add a dark bristled crest running from the nape to the withers. Re-anchor the tail at the rump behind the hip, angle it down-and-back, and give it a soft-furred outline with a clean white distal third rather than a bristle fan with a terminal dot.

rows.readsAs: A small tan dog or a stubby weasel — there is no rodent signal in this picture at all
rows.headWhy: Completely generic, and it is the SAME head as the Marten in this very batch — identical brown domed skull, identical small round ear, identical single white-ringed eye, identical short snub muzzle. The two are directly swappable. The mustRead large orange incisors do not exist: the mouth is a closed dark line, so nothing says gnawing animal.
rows.defect: 1) No incisors — a muskrat/coypu is defined by the pair of orange chisel teeth showing below the lip line. 2) No scaly rope tail: what is drawn is a short thin tapering curl about a fifth of body length, smooth and hairless-looking, where the reference calls for a long, thick, visibly ringed/scaly rope roughly as long as the body. 3) No webbing: the hind feet are plain rounded pegs identical to the front feet, with no splayed elongated toes. 4) The head is too small and too high-set on a visible neck — a semi-aquatic rodent has a blunt wedge head running almost straight into the shoulders with little neck. 5) The torso is a smooth featureless barrel with no rump-high, hunched posture.
rows.fix: Give it two prominent orange incisors projecting below the upper lip and a blunt rounded rostrum to carry them. Replace the tail with a long, thick-at-base rope at least 80% of body length, rendered with cross-hatched scale banding and a hairless matte value distinct from the coat. Redraw the hind feet larger than the front with 4-5 long splayed toes joined by webbing. Sink the neck so the skull sits low and forward of the shoulders, and raise the rump above the withers for the hunched semi-aquatic stance.

rows.readsAs: A dachshund-proportioned weasel — the long low body and bushy tail get it into the mustelid family, but nothing narrows it to a marten
rows.headWhy: Generic, and it is a straight duplicate of the Marsh Rodent's head in this same batch: same domed brown skull, same small round ear, same lone white eye ring, same short muzzle. Swapping the two heads would be invisible. The mustRead pale orange throat bib — the one marking that separates a marten from every other mustelid — is entirely missing, and the face is not foxy: the muzzle is a stubby snub, not a pointed fox wedge.
rows.defect: 1) No throat bib. The chest and throat are the same uniform tan as the flank. 2) Head is duplicated from the Marsh Rodent and the muzzle is too short/blunt to read foxy. 3) The tail is a thin bristle fan, not a bushy full-length brush — it is too sparse, too straight, and it terminates in an odd pale round blob that reads as a lit match head rather than fur. 4) The four legs are identical stubby dowels set at the corners of a sausage, with no ankle, no elbow and no paw shape; a marten's forefeet are broad and the animal is semi-plantigrade so the heel should touch down.
rows.fix: Paint a clearly bounded pale orange bib from the chin down over the throat and upper chest, with a soft irregular lower edge against the darker coat. Lengthen and narrow the muzzle into a fox wedge and enlarge the ear into a broad rounded cup set wide on the skull so it stops matching the rodent head. Thicken the tail to roughly 1.5x the body's depth with a soft outer fur contour rather than radiating straws, and remove the pale terminal blob. Add elbow and hock joints, broaden the forepaws, and let the hind foot flatten to the ground so the plantigrade stance shows.

rows.readsAs: A pale foal, lamb or young goat standing on four legs — nothing about it says meerkat
rows.headWhy: Generic. A cream dome with a slightly pointed muzzle and one dark eye — the same head the Llama is wearing in this batch, and swapping them would go completely unnoticed. The dark eye rings that are the meerkat's signature are at best a faint smudge, and the ears are effectively invisible rather than being small dark crescents set low on the sides of the skull.
rows.defect: The posture is wrong at the root: the spec says upright sentinel and the render is a plain quadruped standing square on four long slender legs with a horizontal back. That single error destroys the read. On top of it: no tripod support from the tail; the tail is a short pale upward curl about a quarter of body length with no black tip, where it should be a long thin tapering rope of nearly body length ending in a dark point; no dark eye mask; legs are far too long and too thin, giving a hooved-ungulate silhouette instead of a short-limbed, pot-bellied, clawed digger; feet are smooth caps with no long digging claws.
rows.fix: Re-pose to the sentinel stance: rotate the spine to vertical, tuck the forelimbs short and close to the chest with the paws hanging at belly height, plant the hind feet flat and plantigrade, and run the tail down and back to the ground as the third leg of a tripod. Shorten and thicken all four limbs substantially. Draw dark elongated rings around each eye and a dark nose. Give the tail a long thin taper with a black terminal third, and add four long curved claws on each forefoot.

rows.readsAs: A grey goat-antelope hybrid — a hornless-bodied donkey with two pale ram horns stuck on the back of the skull.
rows.headWhy: Strip the horns and this is the identical head to Oryx and Pampas Fox: same wedge muzzle with the same little down-turned lip, same flat forehead, same eye set at the same height, same jawline. Nothing about the skull says nilgai — no heavy Roman nose, no narrow tapering face, and the required throat beard tuft is entirely absent. The horns are also the wrong horns: they sweep up and back in a curve when a nilgai's are short, straight and angled FORWARD, and they root too far back on the crown so they read as an accessory rather than as bone growing out of the frontal.
rows.defect: Three anatomy misses. (1) Horn shape and root are wrong — curved, backward, and mounted behind the ears instead of short straight forward spikes rising just above the eye line. (2) No throat beard tuft, which is the one silhouette cue that separates a nilgai from any generic antelope. (3) The topline is level-to-humped, not the strong shoulder-high slope falling away to a low croup that the species is built on. Also: the tail is a hairline stalk that terminates in a detached grey ellipse with a visible gap between them — the tip is floating, not attached.
rows.fix: Re-root the horns forward of the ears at the brow ridge and make them short straight cones angled ~30 degrees forward of vertical. Hang a wedge of longer hair off the underside of the neck at the throat as a beard tuft. Raise the withers ~12% and drop the sacrum so the spine reads as one continuous downhill line from shoulder to tail root. Weld the tail switch to the stalk — continue the stalk into the blob so hair flares out of it rather than sitting near it.

rows.readsAs: A tan calf or a stocky short-legged dog wearing a coat printed with paw-print clip-art.
rows.headWhy: Generic round small-mammal head — a dome, a stub muzzle, two small round ears and one big eye. It carries none of the two required black cheek stripes, no broad feline cheek flare, no short blunt cat nose. Put this same head on the Otter and only the colour would change; the shape is interchangeable.
rows.defect: The rosette generator has produced literal paw-print glyphs — clusters of a pad-shaped blob with four toe dots above it, repeated across the flank. That is the single most damaging thing in the image; it reads as a printed pattern, not as an animal's coat. Underneath that, the body is not a cat: barrel-chested calf proportions with a straight level back, straight tube legs of equal thickness top to bottom ending in blunt cut-off stumps with no paw, no toes and no ankle. No cheek stripes.
rows.fix: Kill the paw glyph entirely. Build rosettes as open elongated rings — a dark broken outline around a coat-coloured centre — and chain them nose-to-tail into 4-5 long streaks that follow the flank's flow line from shoulder to hip. Rebuild the limbs as feline: taper the forelimb from a deep chest, add a visible elbow and hock break, and terminate in a soft rounded pad foot with 3-4 toe lobes. Deepen the chest and tuck the belly so the waist is narrower than the ribcage. Add the two black stripes arcing from the outer eye corner back across each cheek.

rows.readsAs: A brown foal that someone painted zebra stripes on — but on the wrong end.
rows.headWhy: The two dark round ossicone knobs on the crown are unique in this batch and would be noticed instantly if swapped onto any other animal here. That said, the credit is carried entirely by those two knobs — the skull beneath them is the same generic wedge muzzle shared with Nilgai, Oryx and Pampas Fox, and the face has been striped, which is flatly wrong for an okapi.
rows.defect: The striping is on the wrong half of the body. Stripes cover the neck, muzzle, shoulder and mid-flank, and the hindquarters and upper hind legs — the only place an okapi is striped — are left plain brown. Compounding it, the stripes are dark brown/black on a brown ground when they must be near-white on chocolate, so even where they land they barely register. The 'stripes' are also rendered as a fringe of thin parallel hairs feathering off the mid-body edge into open space rather than as bands wrapping around a solid form.
rows.fix: Move the entire stripe field behind the last rib: horizontal cream bands wrapping the rump, hip and upper hind leg only, fading out at the hock. Clear every stripe off the face, neck and shoulder. Raise the stripe value to near-white so it separates from the chocolate ground. Make each band a wrapping shape that curves with the barrel's cross-section and terminates at the body silhouette instead of feathering past it. Give the face the dark okapi mask with pale cheeks and let the ossicones taper into short backward-leaning skin-covered cones rather than mushroom knobs.

rows.readsAs: A cream antelope in swimming goggles.
rows.headWhy: The pair of very long ridged rapier horns sweeping back is decisive — swap this head onto anything else here and it is noticed. But the horns are doing all the work: the skull under them is pixel-for-pixel the same wedge as Nilgai's, and the 'facial mask' has collapsed into two flat black discs sitting on the cheeks like goggles instead of a connected mask.
rows.defect: (1) The black facial mask is rendered as two isolated round blobs. An oryx mask is a connected graphic — a dark blaze down the nose bridge, a band across the brow, and a stripe running down through the eye to the muzzle. As two circles it reads as an accessory, not as markings. (2) The bold black leg markings are entirely missing; the legs are plain cream. (3) Two soft grey ellipses sit on the shoulder and haunch as pasted-on smudges with their own edges — they read as bald patches or dirt rather than as muscle mass under the coat. (4) Same defect as Nilgai: the tail is a hairline that ends in a detached grey ellipse with a gap.
rows.fix: Rebuild the mask as one connected black graphic: nose blaze + brow band + a vertical bar through each eye, all joined. Add black bands at the knee/hock and a dark stripe down the front of each leg, plus a dark line along the flank/belly join. Replace the two grey ellipses with shading that follows the barrel's form and has no edge of its own — light the scapula and the hip as raised volumes, don't stamp ovals on them. Attach the tail switch to the stalk.

rows.readsAs: A pale ferret or a very short-legged stretched cat with a dark head.
rows.headWhy: Small rounded dome with a stub muzzle and tiny ears — the same basic head as the Ocelot, just smaller and darker. The only otter-specific cue present is a few whisker lines. There is no broad flat-topped skull, no wide blunt rhinarium, no eyes-and-ears-high-on-the-head placement that says semi-aquatic. It would swap onto the Ocelot without much notice.
rows.defect: (1) The tail is a thin rope of roughly constant width curling up behind. An otter's tail is the thickest part of the animal at its root — a muscular rudder as deep as the hips that tapers over its full length to a point. As drawn it reads as a cat tail and destroys the species read. (2) The head is dark brown while the entire body is pale cream, and the boundary is abrupt at the neck — it reads as two animals joined, not as one coat. (3) The limbs are four short featureless stubs with no foot at all — no webbed toes, no plantar surface. (4) The body is a straight uniform tube with no shoulder or hip mass showing through, and it sits very small in the frame.
rows.fix: Rebuild the tail: start it as wide as the hips where it leaves the body, keep it thick through the first half, then taper to a point — and give it a slight downward S rather than a cat curl. Bring the body colour up to the head's dark brown and let the pale go only to the throat and chin as a bib. Add short webbed feet with visible toe lobes that splay on the ground plane. Push a shoulder and a hip bulge through the tube so the spine reads as flexible. Scale the animal up in frame.

rows.readsAs: A pale pony or a small deer with a bottlebrush tail — not a canid at all.
rows.headWhy: Same wedge skull as Nilgai and Oryx with a slightly narrower nose and a small dark ear. The ear is neither large nor triangular enough to carry the fox read, the muzzle is a blunt ungulate wedge rather than a long narrow canid snout, and the eye sits in the ungulate position, high and lateral, instead of forward-facing. Swap it onto the hornless Nilgai and few would notice.
rows.defect: The limb type is wrong for the family. The legs are long, straight, stilty and ungulate-proportioned, and they terminate in dark rounded blobs that read as hooves — a fox must stand on four digitigrade paws with visible toes. Combined with the level back and the deep barrel, the whole body is a hoofed animal's. Secondary: the two grey smudge ellipses on shoulder and haunch again read as pasted-on patches; the tail brush is a fan of straight radiating hairs that reads as a bottlebrush or a horse tail rather than a dense bushy fox brush, and it lacks the required dark tip.
rows.fix: Swap in the canid limb: shorter legs with a clear elbow, a sharply angled hock, a pastern, and a compact digitigrade paw with four toe lobes and small claws. Lengthen and narrow the muzzle to a true fox snout and rotate the eyes forward. Enlarge the ears into tall triangles with a broad base. Rebuild the tail as a volume — an ovoid mass of fur around a central stalk, widest at mid-length, with a distinctly dark tip — instead of radiating straight lines. Remove the smudge ellipses and grizzle the back with mixed grey/black banding while keeping the legs tawny.

rows.readsAs: A Belted Galloway calf, or a black-and-white tapir. Not a bear.
rows.headWhy: The eye patch and the round grey ear make it unswappable within this batch, but only the MARKINGS carry that — the underlying head is the same long snouty wedge as the ungulates in this batch, with a protruding muzzle and a down-turned lip. A panda skull is a short, very wide, near-circular dome with the muzzle almost flush to the face. And the patch itself is a plain grey circle, not the black teardrop that slants down and out from the eye.
rows.defect: (1) The legs are white/pale with grey hoof-like feet. A panda's forelegs and hind legs are solid black to the foot, and the feet must be broad plantigrade soles with toes and claws contacting the ground flat — these are cut-off ungulate stumps. (2) There is an extra black band across the rump/haunch in addition to the shoulder band, which is exactly what turns the read into a belted cow. (3) The body is a level-backed barrel with a defined waist, not the round low-slung bulky mass a panda is. (4) The muzzle is far too long and the head too small relative to the body given headFrac 0.29. (5) The white tail called for in the reference is not visible.
rows.fix: Fill the forelegs and hind legs solid black from the shoulder band and hip down through the feet, and replace the stumps with broad flat plantigrade soles showing toe pads and claws. Delete the rear band — the only black band is the shoulder collar joining the two forelegs. Shorten the muzzle drastically so it barely projects past the cheek line, and widen the skull into a near-circle with the two round black ears set wide on the top corners. Make each eye patch a black teardrop angled down and outward from the eye, not a grey circle. Round the back into a continuous arc from neck to rump, drop the belly, and add the short white tail stub at the rear.

rows.readsAs: A tan wooden toy deer — a whittled park-gift-shop stag with a forked twig rack
rows.headWhy: The antler rack is doing 100% of the identification. Strip the antlers and the skull is the exact same construction as this batch's Fox: same narrow wedge muzzle with the same rounded pink-grey nose bulb, same small dark rounded ear, same oversized white-ringed cartoon eyeball set high on the cheek. No elk-specific brow ridge, no long dished face, no heavy Roman nasal bone, no dark facial mask against a pale muzzle. Swap it with the Fox head and nobody would notice.
rows.defect: Three things: (1) the torso is not one solid — a hard-edged rectangular slab sits over the mid-back with visible straight seams at the shoulder and the flank, so the barrel reads as two stacked boxes rather than a ribcage tapering into a loin; (2) the rump patch is a DARK brown blob exactly where the pale cream rump patch belongs — the value is inverted; (3) the neck is a smooth clean tube with no shaggy mane at all, and the antlers are short upright forks rather than the long backswept beam-and-tine rack.
rows.fix: Rebuild the torso as one continuous solid: deep brisket at the elbow, high withers hump behind the neck, ribcage tapering to a tucked loin, then rounded haunch — no straight seams anywhere on the silhouette. Flip the rump patch to pale cream (lighter than the body) and let it wrap the tail base and the back of the thigh. Add the mane as an actual silhouette change: a dark shaggy fringe hanging below the neckline from throat to brisket, breaking the neck's outline. Re-cut the antlers as two long main beams sweeping BACK over the shoulders past the withers with tines branching upward off the beam.

rows.readsAs: A pale ceramic burro or a jackrabbit with a sea-urchin stuck to its rear
rows.headWhy: The two enormous ovoid ears — nearly the height of the whole head and body-tall in silhouette — are unmistakable and could not be moved onto any other animal here. Everything below the ears is generic though: the skull is a small pale cone with a thread-thin snout, no cheek ruff, no dark eye-line, and the eye is a tiny dot instead of the huge dark nocturnal eye the reference calls for.
rows.defect: The tail is the killer — it is a flat radial FAN of stiff white spikes splayed outward from a disc at the hip, reading as a palm frond, a shell, or a shaving brush seen end-on. It is not a tail: no cylindrical core, no root continuous with the rump, no black tip. Second, the body is wrong for a fennec: a short high-backed barrel on four stubby cone legs with a level dorsal line reads as a hoofed foal, not a tiny slender low-slung fox. Third, the ears sprout from the top of the neck rather than from the skull.
rows.fix: Rebuild the tail as a 3D tapering cylinder rooted INTO the rump silhouette, sweeping down and back to roughly hock level, with fur worked around the volume (not radiating from a point) and a distinct black tip. Lower and lengthen the body: shallow chest, long slender back, visible waist tuck, and thin legs with small dark paw pads — total height should let the ears read as a full third of the standing height. Reseat the ear bases on the SKULL just behind the eyes, and enlarge the eye into a big dark round pupil with a dark line running from eye to muzzle.

rows.readsAs: A cream sausage dog, or a hot-dog bun on four stumps with a bear cub's head glued on
rows.headWhy: A small brown ball with one round ear, a blunt nose dot and a big white-ringed eye — this is the identical head part used on the Fur Seal in this same batch, and swapping the two would go completely unnoticed. Nothing mustelid: no wedge-shaped flattened skull, no low-set ears riding wide on a broad braincase, no long neck continuous with the head.
rows.defect: The torso is a perfectly uniform extruded cylinder — same diameter from the armpit to the tail base, dead-straight top line, dead-straight bottom line. There is zero shoulder mass and zero haunch: the legs are stumps punched into the underside of a tube. The tail is a small feather-duster brush pinned ABOVE the back line at the rear corner rather than growing out of the rump, and it ends in a white blob tip. The coat is pale cream where the reference wants dark grizzled, and the brown head against the cream body reads as a mask rather than one animal.
rows.fix: Give the tube an actual skeleton: raise a scapular hump over the forelimb, narrow the waist behind the ribs, then swell a rounded haunch over the hind limb so the top line arches and the belly curves up into a tuck. Root the tail at the base of the spine at rump height so its top edge continues the back line, and make it a thick cylinder tapering to a point — bushy at the base, no white tip. Darken the whole coat to near-black-brown with lighter grizzled guard-hair tips over the shoulders, and carry that same dark value onto the head so the mask disappears. Flatten the skull into a wedge and set the round ears low and wide.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat kid, or an appaloosa lamb — a barnyard animal, not a cat
rows.headWhy: The head is a featureless sphere with no muzzle projection at all, carrying one big round ear mounted on the SIDE of the skull like a mouse's. The only cat cue in the entire picture is the yellow vertical-slit eye, and one iris cannot carry a species. Drop this head onto the Fisher's body and the swap would be invisible.
rows.defect: Nothing here is feline. The legs are four straight rigid dowels dropping vertically from a barrel body and terminating in blunt rounded stumps — no paws, no toes, no digitigrade angle, no crouch. The body is a level-backed barrel with no deep chest and no scapula ridge. The tail is invisible — just a dark nub at the rump — where the reference asks for a short THICK tail. The spotting is randomly scattered dalmatian confetti with no organisation, and the neck stripes are absent entirely.
rows.fix: Rebuild on cat architecture: digitigrade limbs with a real hock angle behind and a wrist break in front, ending in visible four-toed paws that widen at the ground. Deepen the chest below the elbow and let the belly tuck up hard in front of a rounded haunch, with the shoulder blade reading as a bump above the back line. Give the skull a short blunt but PRESENT muzzle with a wide cheek and heavy whisker pad, set both eyes forward on the face, and move the ears to the top of the skull as short rounded triangles. Reorganise the spots into longitudinal ROWS following the body's length and add three or four dark stripes running down the neck onto the shoulders. Extend the tail into a visible short thick club with dark rings.

rows.readsAs: An elephant — instantly. A slightly cartoonish young elephant with a very big eye
rows.headWhy: Trunk, downward tusks and the broad dark ear panel make this unswappable with anything in the batch. That said, the identification is coming entirely from those three appendages: the underlying skull has no domed forehead, no brow shelf and no cheekbone, so the trunk appears to leave a flat blank face plane.
rows.defect: The eye is the loudest error — a large round cartoon eyeball with a bright white sclera ring and a specular highlight, set on the cheek. An elephant's eye is small, dark, wet-looking and buried in heavy wrinkled lids; the reference row even specifies small eyes. Second, proportion: the head/shoulder mass is roughly 40% of the animal and rides very high and far forward, while the legs are short stubby posts — so the beast looks squashed and top-heavy instead of standing tall on pillars. Third, the head merges into the back with no distinct skull dome, so there is no separation between cranium and withers.
rows.fix: Shrink the eye to a small dark almond with no white sclera, sink it into a fold of wrinkled skin, and drop it to sit just above and behind the trunk root. Lengthen all four legs by roughly a third into straight weight-bearing columns so the belly clears the ground by more than a leg's diameter, and shrink the head to about a quarter of the body length. Sculpt a domed forehead with a shallow dip above the trunk root and a visible brow shelf, and put a clear notch between the back of the skull and the shoulder hump. Round the ear's lower edge into an oval that stops at the jawline.

rows.readsAs: An orange toy horse or a whippet in fox paint — the tail reads as a feather duster
rows.headWhy: Same construction as the Elk's head with the antlers removed: small wedge skull, protruding pale nose bulb, oversized white-ringed eye, tiny dark rounded ear nubs. There is no fox marker anywhere — no wide cheek ruff flaring behind the jaw, no big sharp triangular ears with black backs, no white throat, no dark tear-line. Swap it with the de-antlered Elk head and nobody would spot it.
rows.defect: The body is the same featureless extruded cylinder as the Fisher's — constant diameter, flat top line, flat belly, no chest depth, no shoulder blade, no haunch — and it rides on four long straight dowel legs, so the proportions read equine rather than low and slinking. The tail is a stiff radiating bristle-fan pinned above the rump at a jaunty upward angle; it has a white tip but no cylindrical mass and no continuity with the body, and at maybe a third of body length it is far short of the near-body-length brush required. The ears are undersized rounded nubs, not sharp triangles.
rows.fix: Drop the standing height and stretch the back: shallow slinking body with a deep-but-narrow chest, a real waist tuck, and shorter legs so the belly sits low. Sculpt shoulder and haunch swellings into the top line. Rebuild the tail as a heavy cylindrical mass rooted at the rump and carried low, roughly as long as the body, widening in the middle before tapering to a clean white tip — fur strokes should wrap the volume, not radiate from a hub. Enlarge the ears to tall sharp triangles about half the head length, with dark backs. Add the white cheek and throat and a cream belly against the rust flanks, and keep the black stockings, which already work.

rows.readsAs: A stubby capybara or a bear cub — a land mammal on four short legs, with nothing marine about it
rows.headWhy: Identical part to the Fisher's head in this batch: small brown ball, one round ear, big white-ringed eye, tiny nose dot. Swapping the two would be undetectable. Missing every pinniped cue — no long dog-like projecting muzzle, no bulging mystacial whisker pad, no whiskers at all, and the ear reads as a round bear ear rather than a small furled external flap.
rows.defect: The defining feature is simply absent: there are no fore-flippers. The forelimbs are two short stubby posts identical to the hind ones, so the chest is not propped up and the animal stands level like a rodent. The torso is the same constant-diameter cylinder used across this batch — no barrel chest, no taper toward a small pelvis. The hind limbs do have some toe division but they hang straight down as legs rather than rotating forward as flippers under the body.
rows.fix: Replace the forelimbs with long broad oar-shaped fore-flippers — nearly a third of body length, naked-looking leading edge, angled back and outward — and use them to LIFT the chest so the shoulders sit clearly higher than the hips and the head is carried above the back line. Taper the torso: big barrel chest at the flippers narrowing to a small pelvis. Rotate the hind flippers forward under the body, splayed flat on the ground with visible long digits. Rebuild the head with a long projecting dog muzzle, a domed forehead, a fat whisker pad and a spray of long pale whiskers, and shrink the ear to a small backswept furled tube low on the skull.

rows.readsAs: A dark stocky cartoon bull or buffalo with an oversized pale hoop earring looped across its face
rows.headWhy: The only thing distinguishing this head is the horn prop, and the horn is drawn wrong — a closed cream ring that arcs forward and CROSSES the muzzle, plus a second crescent floating behind it. Strip the hoop and the skull is the same dark rounded wedge with a dark eye smudge and two small dark ear nubs used on the Goat. Nothing in the cranium says bovine: no broad flat frontal bone, no wide moist boxy muzzle, no dewlap.
rows.defect: Three of three mustReads fail and the horns are geometrically broken. (1) The horns form a closed loop that overlaps the front of the face instead of two crescents springing from the outer corners of the forehead and sweeping OUT then UP; one horn also occludes the muzzle it should sit well above. (2) There is no shoulder ridge — the topline is a smooth barrel with the highest point mid-back, when the gaur's defining silhouette is a tall muscular ridge over the withers that drops abruptly to the loin. (3) No white stockings: all four legs are the same grey-tan as the body, and (4) no pale grey forehead patch — the forehead is the darkest area of the head. The haunch is also a flat darker ellipse stamped onto the flank rather than modeled mass.
rows.fix: Reroot the horns at the outer top corners of the skull, above and behind the eye, as two open crescents that sweep laterally then curve up and inward — never let horn geometry cross the muzzle silhouette. Rebuild the topline: raise the withers into a distinct ridge peaking just behind the neck join and taper it down to a lower hip, so the back reads as a wedge not an oval. Add a boxy squared muzzle and a throat/brisket dewlap. Paint the lower quarter of each leg white with a hard cuff line at the knee/hock, and lighten the forehead between the horn bases to pale grey so it reads as a mask.

rows.readsAs: A generic cream antelope or young deer — pleasant, but nothing names the species
rows.headWhy: This head and the Gerenuk's are the same asset at the same scale: identical cream wedge, identical dark eye pip with the same dark nose dab, identical small ears tucked at the horn base, identical pale horns. Swap them and no one could tell. The horns are the only species signal and they are drawn as two smooth featureless prongs — no annulations, so they read as a wishbone rather than a gazelle's ringed lyre.
rows.defect: Horns are un-ringed smooth tapers and they rise almost straight and parallel; the gazelle lyre curves back, then out, then the tips hook forward and inward — none of that S is present. The dark lateral flank band is entirely missing, so tan and white never separate and the body reads as one flat cream mass. The haunch is a hard-edged darker circle pasted on the hip like a sticker rather than a muscle bulge, and the shoulder has a matching disc — both read as holes. The neck is also too short and too thick for the mustRead's 'long neck'.
rows.fix: Cut 8–12 raised annulation rings into the lower two-thirds of each horn (a repeating light/dark ridge band), then bend the horn: back-sweep from the base, flare apart at mid-length, hook the tips forward. Run a hard-edged dark chocolate band along the lower flank from the elbow to the stifle with clean white below it and tan above — that one stripe carries the whole silhouette. Replace the pasted haunch/shoulder discs with soft-edged gradient bulges whose light comes from the same direction as the body's, and lengthen the neck by roughly a head-length while narrowing it.

rows.readsAs: The gazelle above with its neck stretched — a giraffe-necked antelope only by accident of proportion
rows.headWhy: This is the most literal instance of the owner's complaint in the batch: the head is not merely similar to the Gazelle's, it is visually the same object — same cream wedge, same horn pair, same eye pip, same nose dab, same ear size. The one feature that would have made it unmistakable, the huge round radar ears, is absent; the ears are the same small tucked triangles as the gazelle's.
rows.defect: The species reads only through neck length; every other cue fails. (1) The mustRead's 'huge ears' are missing — gerenuk ears are enormous, wide, rounded and held out sideways, and here they are tiny nubs hidden at the horn base. (2) The head should be a tiny narrow wedge on that long neck; at this size it is the same head volume as the Gazelle's, so the head-to-neck ratio does not read as extreme. (3) The horns are wrong for the species AND identical to the neighbour's — gerenuk horns are short, thick, heavily ridged and hook sharply forward at the tip, not tall smooth prongs. (4) Body and haunch are the Gazelle's, complete with the same pasted-on dark hip disc, and there is no reddish saddle over a paler underside.
rows.fix: Give this species its own head build: shrink the skull to roughly 60% of the Gazelle's volume, narrow it to a fine wedge, and mount two huge rounded leaf-shaped ears flaring out sideways at nearly 45 degrees — they should be as tall as the skull is long. Replace the horns with short, thick, deeply ridged S-hooks that curve back then snap forward at the tip. Thin the legs to true stilts and slim the barrel so the neck-to-body ratio exaggerates. Add a two-tone coat: rufous saddle over the back, sharply lighter fawn on the flanks and white underneath.

rows.readsAs: A pale grey pig or sausage-dog with a duck's bill and a bottlebrush stuck to its rump
rows.headWhy: The head is the batch's small rounded generic skull with a single large round eye, and the one feature that makes a giant anteater unmistakable at any size — a long straight tapering tube of a snout, roughly as long as the rest of the skull — is instead a short blunt downward-hooking bill. As drawn it could be swapped onto the Otter with almost no one noticing; both are small pale rounded heads with a big round eye and a stub muzzle.
rows.defect: Every mustRead fails. (1) The snout is a stubby hooked bill, not a long tapered tube with a pin-hole mouth; the skull also has a pronounced eye where the anteater's should be a tiny bead set far back. (2) The tail is a sparse fan of straight separate bristles reading as porcupine quills, not an enormous bushy flag — and it does not overlap or shadow the body the way a real flag tail does. (3) There is no black-and-white diagonal shoulder wedge; the animal is a uniform pale grey with no marking at all. (4) The feet are pale blunt hoof-like tips, so the note about knuckle-walking on curled foreclaws is not represented — no claws are visible anywhere. (5) There is a stray pale rounded capsule at the base of the tail that does not attach to anything and reads as a rendering artifact.
rows.fix: Rebuild the head as a single long cone: skull merging into a snout roughly 1.5x skull length, straight-tapered, with a black pin-dot nostril/mouth at the tip and a bead eye set high and far back near the small round ear. Replace the bristle fan with a dense overlapping mass of long hairs that flares to at least body height and reads as one silhouette blob with hair edges, not separate strands, and delete the pale capsule at its root. Paint the black wedge: a thick black band edged in white starting at the chest, rising diagonally across the shoulder and dying out over the back — it is the strongest identifier this animal has. Shorten and thicken the forelegs, tuck the wrist so the foot rests on the knuckles, and show two long curved black claws folded back under the wrist.

rows.readsAs: A dachshund-proportioned weasel or ferret
rows.headWhy: The head is genuinely better differentiated than the ungulates' — small, rounded, low-set round ears, a blunt short muzzle and a large forward round eye do read mustelid rather than hoofstock. But within the carnivore/mustelid family it is fully generic: no whisker pads, no whiskers at all despite 'whiskered head' in the reference, no flattening of the crown, and no cream bib to anchor it, so it could serve as a weasel, mink, mongoose or river otter unchanged.
rows.defect: The single most important identifier is drawn as its explicit counter-example: the tail is a thin, round, tapering rope curving up off the rump — exactly the river-otter tail the note warns against — instead of a broad, dorsoventrally flattened rudder that is widest at mid-length and finishes in a spade. The cream throat bib is absent, so the whole animal is one uniform tan tube. The legs are four short blunt stumps with no paw structure and no webbing, and the torso has no shoulder or haunch mass at all — it is a straight cylinder with the same diameter from neck to hip, which flattens the animal into a pipe.
rows.fix: Redraw the tail as a wide flat paddle: narrow at the root, widening to roughly a third of body depth by mid-length, with a visible flat upper plane catching light and a spade tip — keep it low and trailing, not raised in a rope curve. Add the cream bib as an irregular blotchy patch under the chin and across the throat with a ragged border (the blotch shape is individual to the species and instantly names it). Build real shoulder and hip masses into the cylinder so the topline undulates, and finish each limb with a splayed webbed paw showing five short toes. Add three or four whisker strokes off each side of the muzzle.

rows.readsAs: A giraffe — immediately and unambiguously
rows.headWhy: This is the one head in the batch nobody could swap. The long narrow tapering face, the eye set high and far back, the small rounded muzzle knob, and above all the pair of dark ossicone knobs on the crown are all species-specific, and the reticulated pattern carries up the neck onto the skull so the head is visually continuous with the animal.
rows.defect: Two anatomy issues remain, both minor. The ossicones fuse into a single dark fuzzy blob across the top of the skull rather than reading as two separate skin-covered knobs with a gap between them and a tuft on each. And the reticulated patch pattern stops at the top of the limbs — the legs are plain flat cream from shoulder to hoof — where a real giraffe carries patches down the upper leg, fading out only near the fetlock; the abrupt boundary makes the legs look like separate unpainted parts. The back-slope from withers to hips is also shallower than the mustRead calls for, so the body reads as an oval rather than a wedge.
rows.fix: Split the ossicones into two distinct cylinders set apart by about one eye-width, each with its own dark terminal tuft and a visible gap of pale skull between them. Carry the reticulation onto the upper foreleg and thigh, letting the polygon size shrink and the pattern dissolve into plain cream around the knee/hock rather than stopping with a hard line at the body edge. Raise the withers slightly and drop the croup so the topline slopes visibly from shoulder to hip.

rows.readsAs: A sheep or a lamb — precisely the animal the reference note says it must not be mistaken for
rows.headWhy: There are no horns. The two small dark curved nubs on the crown read as ears, not horns, so the skull is left as a plain pale rounded wedge with a dark eye patch and a pale muzzle — the same construction as the Gaur's minus the hoop, and recolorable into any of the ungulates in this batch. Nothing on it is caprine: no beard, no long straight nose bridge, no rectangular pupil visible, no horns.
rows.defect: All three mustReads fail and the note's specific anti-sheep warning is triggered on every point. (1) No backward-sweeping horns — the head is hornless. (2) No chin beard. (3) The tail is a small dark blob hanging DOWN on the rump, when the goat's tail must point up and be flicked over the rump; a down tail plus the woolly-looking flank is exactly the sheep silhouette. The body is also over-round and bulging — the barrel reads as a fleece rather than the goat's flatter, more angular frame — and the shoulder and haunch again appear as flat pasted-on discs rather than modeled mass. The cloven hooves are correct and are the only species-appropriate feature present.
rows.fix: Add horns: two ribbed cones rising from just behind the eye line and sweeping back and slightly outward over the neck, clearly separate from and larger than the ears, with visible transverse ridges. Add a wedge of long hair hanging from the chin. Flip the tail to a short upright stub angled up and away from the rump, with the pale rump patch visible beneath it. Flatten the barrel and straighten the topline so the frame reads angular rather than fleecy, straighten and narrow the face profile, and replace the pasted shoulder/haunch discs with soft-edged mass.

rows.readsAs: A fennec fox crossed with a donkey foal — tan stick-legged ungulate with two enormous dark round ears
rows.headWhy: Unique in the batch only because of the two oversized dark-brown ROUND ears that dominate the skull — but they are the wrong ears entirely. A caracal ear is a narrow triangle, black on the back, with a 5cm black tuft trailing off the tip; here they are giant rounded fennec paddles with no tuft. Under the ears the head itself is a tiny featureless tan cone shared with Chamois/Cheetah.
rows.defect: Three anatomy failures compound. (1) Ears: round, oversized, untufted — the single mustRead feature (black trailing tuft) is absent. (2) Feet: all four limbs are straight tapered rods ending in dark hoof-toned caps, identical to the Chamois in this same batch — there is no digitigrade paw, no toe pads, no ankle break. A cat is standing on hooves. (3) Skull is far too small relative to headFrac 0.23 and sits on a straight neck with no feline shoulder blade; the topline is a flat unbroken plank from withers to rump with no shoulder or haunch mass, and the long powerful hind legs are the same length and thickness as the front.
rows.fix: Rebuild the ear as a tall narrow black-backed triangle roughly 40% of head height, and draw the tuft as 4-6 stiff black hairs continuing PAST the ear apex on the same axis — silhouette hair, not a fill. Swap the hoof cap for the feline paw primitive (round pad, three visible toe lobes, foot bending forward off a raised heel), and raise the hock joint on the hind limb so the rear leg reads as a crouched Z, not a post. Enlarge the skull ~25% and add a shoulder-blade bulge behind it.

rows.readsAs: A caribou or reindeer — the only picture in this batch that names itself correctly
rows.headWhy: Genuinely specific: branched palmate antlers with a forward-projecting brow tine, a dark bulbous rhinarium on a blunt down-turned muzzle, a dark eye ringed in white set high on the skull, and the head carried below the topline. Nothing else in the batch could wear it.
rows.defect: The coat is not on the body. The shaggy fur reads as a fringe of separate stiff straw-coloured spikes tacked around the OUTSIDE of the silhouette — along the spine, down the brisket, under the belly — pointing outward like glued hay rather than lying along a surface. Nothing on the interior of the flank carries the same texture, so the animal looks like a smooth shape with a wig stapled to its edge. Separately, the haunch is a flat lighter-grey CIRCLE pasted onto the rump with a hard visible boundary — a disc, not a muscle mass; it reads as a hole or a brand. The hooves are also narrow dark points, missing the wide splayed snowshoe spread the row calls for.
rows.fix: Kill the outline fringe and re-emit fur as short directional strokes that follow the body's form field across the whole flank, letting only the neck ruff and brisket break the silhouette — and make those break it in clumped wedges (3-5 strokes per clump) rather than as evenly spaced single spikes. Replace the haunch disc with a soft-edged value ramp whose light side faces the same key as the shoulder. Widen the hoof to a splayed two-toe crescent about 1.6x the pastern width.

rows.readsAs: A grey shorthair cat wearing a dirty saddle blanket
rows.headWhy: Specific within this batch: small round short-muzzled skull, two upright triangular ears set wide on the crown, and a bright yellow eye with a visible vertical slit — the only slit pupil here. It could not be swapped onto any of the ungulates. The weakness is that it is specific mostly by ear shape and eye colour; the muzzle itself is a plain nub with no whisker pad, nose triangle, or the whiskers the row requires.
rows.defect: The tabby marking has failed into a pasted-on object. A dark brown streaked slab sits across the back and upper flank with HARD straight-cut boundaries — a flat top edge along the spine, a squared-off leading edge at the shoulder, a ragged bottom edge floating in mid-flank — and its colour (warm dirty brown) is unrelated to the cool grey body, so it reads as a separate blanket or a patch of matted straw laid over the cat rather than as fur growing out of it. The stripes inside it run as parallel diagonal streaks that ignore the curve of the ribcage. Secondary: the legs are four featureless grey cylinders with no paw, no toes and no ankle; the whiskers listed in mustRead are entirely absent.
rows.fix: Recolour the tabby to a value shift of the base grey (same hue, ~30% darker) instead of a foreign brown, dissolve the slab's hard perimeter so markings taper out into the coat, and re-lay the stripes as vertical bands that WRAP the barrel — narrowing and curving as they cross the ribs, breaking into spots down the flank. Add a paw at each foot and 5-6 whiskers per side, drawn as thin light arcs clearing the head silhouette.

rows.readsAs: A spotted goat or a piebald sheep — not a cow
rows.headWhy: This head is the Chamois head with different horns bolted on. Same long tapering cone muzzle, same upcurved smile line, same large dark eye set at the same height, same small ear tucked behind the horn base. Swap the two heads and the only tell is horn shape. Cattle demand the opposite of what is drawn: a broad boxy skull with a wide FLAT frontal plate, a blunt square muzzle as deep as it is long, and a big flat rhinarium. Here the face tapers to a point.
rows.defect: The body is an egg, not a barrel. The back is a continuous convex arch from neck to tail with no straight level topline, no hip point, no withers; the belly curves up in the same arc so the ribcage has no depth and no floor. Legs are four thin equal-length rods with tiny dark dots for feet — no cloven split, no dewclaw, no cannon-to-fetlock break — and they are set too close together under the middle of the body, which is what pushes the read toward goat. The tail tuft is a smooth grey paddle blob rather than a rope of hair. Colour is also off: the ground coat is bluish-white with a plastic sheen, unlike any cattle hide.
rows.fix: Flatten the topline into a straight run from withers to hip with a distinct hook bone bump at the pelvis, then drop the brisket so the chest floor sits BELOW the elbow and the barrel is visibly deeper than it is tall at the flank. Square the muzzle: widen the nose end to at least 70% of skull width, flatten the frontal between the horns, and delete the smile curve. Split each hoof into two toes with a visible cleft, spread the front pair wider than the hind. Rebuild the tail tuft as splayed hair strands and warm the base coat off blue toward cream.

rows.readsAs: A generic tan deer or young antelope with two little spikes on its head
rows.headWhy: The same head casting as Cattle — long tapering cone muzzle, identical eye size and placement, identical ear stub — differing only in horn geometry and coat colour. Worse, the horns themselves are wrong: they rise as two nearly straight pale prongs angled up and slightly FORWARD, when the chamois's one unmistakable feature is a slender vertical horn that hooks abruptly backward into a hook at the very tip.
rows.defect: Both mustRead identifiers are missing. (1) No backward hook on the horns — they read as young goat spikes. (2) No facial mask: the face is a flat uniform tan with only a slight darkening near the eye, where the chamois requires a hard black stripe running from the ear through the eye to the muzzle over a white cheek and throat, which is the highest-contrast thing on the animal. Anatomically the body is also a smooth featureless barrel with a rounded topline; the haunch appears as a soft dark oval smudge rather than a defined thigh, and the legs are four identical tapered rods with no hock angle.
rows.fix: Redraw the horn as a thin near-vertical shaft that turns through roughly 130 degrees in the top fifth to form a tight rearward hook, and darken it to near-black so it separates from the tan skull. Paint the mask as hard-edged shapes, not a gradient: black band ear-to-muzzle, white cheek panel below it, white throat. Then angle the hind limb — femur forward, tibia back, cannon vertical — so the leg has the springy Z of a mountain antelope instead of a table leg.

rows.readsAs: A spotted fallow-deer fawn, or an Appaloosa foal
rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with the Civet head in this batch: same small tan wedge, same pair of small round side-set ears, same eye, same short blunt nose, differing only in the density of speckles. Nothing on it says cat. The cheetah head has one non-negotiable identifier — the black tear stripe from the inner eye corner down to the lip — and it is not drawn.
rows.defect: This is not a cat's body. (1) Tail: short, thick and curled UPWARD over the rump like a fawn's flag, when the cheetah's tail is the longest relative tail of any big cat — a rudder nearly the length of the body, carried low with a ringed white tip. (2) Chest: the torso is an even sausage of constant depth; there is no deep narrow keel dropping between the forelegs and no whippet tuck at the waist, so the greyhound proportion the note demands is absent. (3) Feet: four straight rods ending in blunt caps toned like hooves, no paws, no toes. (4) Spots: irregular blobs that clump into blotches and patches on the torso only, leaving the legs and most of the head bare, where a cheetah is evenly stippled with small discrete round spots from face to tail across the entire body.
rows.fix: Replace the tail with a long low-carried tail at least 70% of body length, thin and even, with 3-4 dark rings and a white tip. Deepen the chest so the brisket drops below the elbow, then cut the waist in hard behind the ribs to a narrow tuck and raise the hip so the topline slopes down toward the shoulder. Swap the hoof caps for compact paws with semi-retracted claws. Re-scatter the spots as uniformly sized solid circles at even spacing including down the legs and across the crown, and paint the tear stripe as a solid black line from eye corner to lip on both sides of the muzzle.

rows.readsAs: A speckled lamb or a young spotted goat on stilts
rows.headWhy: The same head as the Cheetah in this batch — swap them and no one would notice. Small pale tan wedge, small round side-set ears, one dark eye, blunt short nose. The row's own note insists the muzzle is LONG and POINTED and the face carries dark bands through the eyes; the render has neither. A civet head should read as a mongoose or a small mustelid, never as a hoofstock face.
rows.defect: The build is inverted from what a civet is. The animal stands TALL on four long straight rods with the belly high off the ground, when a palm civet is a low tube of a body carried close to the earth on short legs — the single most recognisable thing about its silhouette. The tail is short and curled up over the back rather than long, thick and trailing behind at roughly body length; it does carry two or three dark bands, which is the one mustRead partly satisfied. There is no facial mask at all, the muzzle is a stub, and the feet are blunt caps with no toes or claws.
rows.fix: Halve the leg length and lengthen the torso to about 2.4x its depth so the body reads as a low tube skimming the ground, with the belly line dropping below mid-leg. Extend the tail to full body length, carry it straight back and low, and keep the banding. Draw the muzzle out into a long narrow point with a small dark nose at the tip and set the eyes further forward on it, then paint hard dark bands across each eye and a pale bar between them. Add five-toed clawed feet.

rows.readsAs: A brown plush teddy-capybara. Nothing in the silhouette says bear.
rows.headWhy: Generic mammal blob: rounded cranium, one small dark round ear stuck on the crown, a big white-sclera cartoon eye, and a short convex snout ending in a dark nose dot. Swap this head onto the Hyrax and nobody would notice — both are the same round-skull/small-round-ear/dot-nose construction at different scales. Nothing ursine: no dished concave profile, no broad heavy muzzle block, no small deep-set eye.
rows.defect: Three of the three mustRead cues are absent. (1) No shoulder hump — the topline is a smooth oval and the highest point sits mid-back/rump, i.e. the black-bear silhouette the note explicitly warns against. (2) The facial profile is convex, not dished; the forehead rounds straight into the snout. (3) No long pale front claws, and worse, the feet are wrong type entirely: all four legs are smooth cylinders ending in narrow dark toe-tips that read as hooves, so the bear is standing on tiptoe instead of on plantigrade soles. Eye is cartoon-large with a bright white sclera, which fights the 'small eyes' spec and the whole species.
rows.fix: Rebuild the topline: put the withers mass at ~35% of body length and drive it 12-15% above the croup so the back reads as a downhill run from shoulder to rump. Cut a concave notch into the profile between brow and muzzle-base, then flatten and broaden the muzzle into a rectangular block. Replace the four hoof-tips with a broad plantigrade foot — a flat sole ellipse wider than the leg, whole rear foot planted heel-to-toe on the ground line, and 4-5 long pale down-curving claws projecting forward past the toes on the front feet. Shrink the eye and drop the white sclera to a dark iris with one small catchlight.

rows.readsAs: A generic tan antelope with a very upright neck — closer to a gerenuk or young impala than a hartebeest.
rows.headWhy: Specific, but only because of the hardware: the pale horns rise off a dark raised bony pedestal, which is a unique silhouette element in this batch. Strip the horns and the head underneath is interchangeable with the Ibex's — same tapered wedge, same eye. The face is also not doing its job (see defect).
rows.defect: The signature cue — an EXTREMELY long narrow face — is only mildly delivered; the muzzle is a moderate taper, roughly the same face-length ratio as the Ibex and Horse in this batch, so the animal loses its single most identifying feature. The compensating length has gone into the NECK instead, which is long and near-vertical and pushes the read toward gerenuk. Horn shape reads as a splayed lyre/V rather than the hartebeest bracket. Ears are not readable at all — they are swallowed by the dark pedestal mass between the horns. The back slope is present and correct.
rows.fix: Move the length from neck to face: shorten the neck ~20% and set it at a 45-55 degree angle instead of near-vertical, then extend the muzzle so the face is 2.5-3x its own depth, keeping the width constant so it reads narrow, not just long. Reshape the horns to the bracket: both rise close together and parallel off the pedestal, kink sharply outward, then hook back toward the tail. Pull two long narrow leaf-shaped ears out clear of the pedestal in a lighter value so they separate from the dark base.

rows.readsAs: A pink-grey dachshund, or a pig with a dog's proportions. No viewer would say hippo.
rows.headWhy: Distinct within the batch — a large faceted wedge with visible planes, unlike any other head here — but distinct for the wrong reasons: it reads as a blocky cartoon dog head. The mouth is a thin curved 'smile' line drawn onto the surface like a decal rather than a modelled jawline, and the eye sits at mid-skull height on the side of the face.
rows.defect: Body proportion is wrong in kind: this is a long shallow tube (roughly 3.5 body-lengths to one body-depth) with a straight belly, where a hippo is an enormous deep barrel about 2:1 with a belly that hangs nearly to the ground. The stumpy pillar legs are right but they are attached to the wrong solid. On the head, all three cues fail: the muzzle is NOT squared and wider than the skull, it tapers; there are no ears at all; and the eyes/ears/nostrils are not stacked on the top plane of the skull — the single visible eye is on the cheek and there is no nostril.
rows.fix: Rebuild the torso as a deep barrel: cut length by ~30%, increase depth ~50%, and drop the belly line to within one hoof-height of the ground so the pillar legs look buried in mass. Flare the muzzle wider than the braincase and square it off with a flat frontal plane. Then put the sensory row on TOP: two small round bump-ears at the back of the skull roof, two eyes on raised orbital knobs just in front of them, and two nostril nubs at the front of the muzzle roof — all four features silhouetted above the head's top contour, which is the pose-reading a hippo lives on. Delete the decal smile; model the mouth as an actual jaw split with a heavy lower lip.

rows.readsAs: A tan horse or foal — the species reads, but a broken one, with a feather-duster glued to its flank.
rows.headWhy: The long tapered muzzle with a nostril dot and a dark brow patch over a white-sclera eye is EXACTLY the head on the Hyena in this same batch. Add rounded ears and it becomes the hyena; that is a direct swap nobody would catch. The equine head has no jowl mass, no cheekbone, and no clearly-separated pricked ear of its own.
rows.defect: (1) The tail is broken: a fan of dark straight bristles is attached low on the flank, overlapping the haunch instead of springing from a high dock at the top of the croup, and a pale bulbous blob — the tail-root ellipse — is z-ordered on top of the hair and offset to the far END of the fan, so the tail terminates in a pale ball. It reads as a broom, not a flowing tail. (2) No mane whatsoever: the neck crest is a bare smooth edge, and the arch is shallow. Legs and single hooves are correct.
rows.fix: Re-anchor the tail: origin at the top of the croup where the topline turns down, hair sweeping down and back in a curved cone that tapers to a point, and put the root ellipse UNDER the hair in draw order (and at the origin, not the tip). Delete the pale bulb. Add a crest mane as a thick strip lying along the whole top of the neck from poll to withers, with a forelock breaking forward over the brow. Give the neck a convex crest curve. Then differentiate the head from the Hyena's: shorter, deeper jowl, a defined cheekbone disc, and two narrow pricked ears angled forward.

rows.readsAs: A spotted appaloosa pony. The spots are the only thing suggesting anything else.
rows.headWhy: Same slender tapered muzzle, same brow patch, same white-sclera eye as the Horse in this batch — the ONLY difference is the pair of rounded dark ears. The ears themselves are correct and well-shaped, but they are the sole species marker on an otherwise borrowed equine head. Swap the two heads and only the ears would give it away.
rows.defect: This is a horse mesh with spots painted on. (1) The signature sloping back is absent — the topline is essentially level, with the shoulder barely above the croup, so the skeletal forequarter dominance the note calls out never appears. (2) The neck is thin and equine, not the thick muscular column a bone-crusher needs, and the jaw is a slender snout with no masseter or jaw depth. (3) Feet are wrong type: slim legs ending in dark hoof-like tips instead of digitigrade paws with visible toes and blunt claws. (4) It inherits the Horse's broken tail — the same bristle fan with the pale root-ellipse blob mislaid at the tip.
rows.fix: Raise the withers ~20% above the croup and shorten the hind limbs relative to the fore so the downhill slope is skeletal and continuous from neck to tail. Thicken the neck to at least the depth of the skull and add a short erect dorsal mane crest along it. Rebuild the skull with a deep wide jaw: heavy masseter bulge behind the eye, short broad muzzle, mouth line ending well back under the eye. Swap all four feet for four-toed digitigrade paws with a heel lifted clear of the ground. Fix the tail with the same treatment as the Horse, but shorter and bushier.

rows.readsAs: A small cream lamb, rendered tiny in the corner of the frame.
rows.headWhy: A small round skull with a dark cap, one tiny dark ear on the crown, a small catchlit eye and a blunt muzzle — the same construction as the Grizzly Bear's head in this batch, just smaller and paler. Nothing about it is hyrax-specific: no whisker field, no visible nose pad, no incisor hint.
rows.defect: (1) The long whiskers in the mustRead are completely absent — no whisker strokes at the muzzle at all. (2) The legs are too long and slim and the belly rides high off the ground, which turns the low-slung guinea-pig body into a leggy lamb; the small rounded ears and taillessness are correct but can't carry the read alone. (3) Framing: the organism occupies roughly a third of the canvas width and sits high and right of centre, wasting most of the 440px frame and shrinking every feature below legibility — a rendering-scale bug, not just a composition preference.
rows.fix: Scale the subject to fill ~75-80% of the frame width and centre it on the ground line. Shorten the legs by ~40% so the belly sits about one leg-length off the ground and the body reads as a low rounded loaf. Add a splayed whisker fan of 5-6 long fine strokes from each side of the muzzle, extending past the head silhouette. Add a small dark rounded nose pad and a slight overhang to the upper lip to sell the blunt rodent-like muzzle.

rows.readsAs: A shaggy cream sheep with straw stuck to it.
rows.headWhy: Small pale wedge skull with a dark eye patch — essentially the Hartebeest's head minus the pedestal. The one thing that should make an ibex head unmistakable, the horns, is a small pale curl hugging the skull that could belong to any ram. No beard, no distinguishing muzzle. Swap it with the Hartebeest head and only the horn hardware would tell.
rows.defect: (1) The horns — the entire species read — are wrong: a short pale curl tucked against the head, curving forward and down, roughly one head-length long. An ibex needs massive scimitars sweeping BACKWARD in a long arc over the neck, at least 1.5-2 head-lengths, with transverse knobbed ridges along the front edge. (2) No goat beard under the chin at all. (3) The coat fringe is an artifact: straight uniform straw-like spikes radiate from the body outline including the belly and the top of the back, reading as hay stuck to the model rather than a shaggy winter coat — they are all the same length and the same straight line, and several detach from the silhouette. Body stockiness and the cloven feet are correct.
rows.fix: Replace the horns with a pair sweeping up from the poll then arcing back over the withers, thick at the base and tapering, with 8-12 raised transverse ridge bands across the outer curve — and give them enough length that the tips clear the shoulder. Hang a wedge-shaped beard from the chin. Rework the coat: vary the fringe strand length and curvature, bias it to follow gravity (down and back, not radiating outward from the belly), keep every strand rooted inside the silhouette, and concentrate the shag on the chest, flank and haunch rather than ringing the whole outline evenly.

rows.readsAs: A shaggy brown ferret-dog plush on four hollow pipes — a toy with the legs cut from tubing.
rows.headWhy: Small round dome, a low round ear, a tapered pinch of a muzzle and one oversized white cartoon eyeball. Strip the color and it is the same skull as the Wombat in this same batch: same dome curve, same round ear, same eye size and placement. Nothing in it says mustelid — no long low-slung head, no heavy jaw muscle, no short rounded ear set almost flush into the fur, no dark bandit mask over pale cheek patches.
rows.defect: All four legs terminate as open cylinders — you can read the darker elliptical bore at the bottom of both front legs and both rear legs. There are no feet at all, let alone the huge clawed paws the species is built around. Secondary anatomy failures: the back is dead level, so the signature humped shoulder mass is missing; there is no pale flank stripe anywhere; and the tail is a dark spiky brush angled DOWN and FORWARD under the body, tipped with a pale rounded blob, so it reads as a dropped club or a bone rather than a bushy tail carried behind.
rows.fix: Cap every limb with an actual wolverine paw: a broad plantigrade-leaning pad wider than the leg shaft, five splayed toes and long pale claws that project past the toe line. Then raise the spine profile — build a shoulder hump peaking above the hip line and drop the head below the hump so the topline runs high-shoulder to low-croup. Add the pale flank band as a light hide zone sweeping from behind the shoulder, along the lower flank, and up over the tail base. Re-aim the tail up and back at 30-40 degrees and make it a thick continuous plume of the same coat, not radiating spikes with a ball on the end.

rows.readsAs: A small pale lamb or a shorn sheep standing on four stilts.
rows.headWhy: It is the Wolverine's head repainted lighter — same round dome, same dark cap, same single round ear blob, same big white round eye at the same height. The thing that should make a wombat unmistakable, the broad bare rhinarium spanning nearly the full width of the muzzle, is not there: the snout tapers to a small pointed tip instead. Swap this head onto the Wolverine body and nobody would flag it.
rows.defect: The digging build is absent. The legs are slender, straight, moderately long posts set vertically under the body, which is what gives the lamb read; a wombat's legs are stumpy, thick, and bowed outward at the elbow and stifle with the feet planted wide of the body line. The barrel also sits too high off the ground for the species. On top of that the muzzle is pointed rather than blunt and bare-nosed, and there is a visible seam where the near foreleg meets the chest, so the limb reads as a separate piece stuck on rather than emerging from shoulder mass.
rows.fix: Shorten every limb by roughly a third and thicken it to at least the depth of the shoulder, then bow it: elbows out, feet planted outside the barrel silhouette, so the body nearly grazes the ground. Terminate each foot in a broad flat five-toe pad with stout digging claws. Rebuild the muzzle as a squared-off block with a wide dark bare nose pad covering most of the front face, and set the small eyes low and close to that nose. Fair the foreleg root into the shoulder mass so no seam is visible.

rows.readsAs: A horned bison or musk-ox that has been rolled in dry straw.
rows.headWhy: The big pale crescent horns, the head carried low below the shoulder hump, and the deep blunt muzzle make this head unmistakable inside this batch — it could not be swapped with the Wombat or the Wolverine. The caveat is that the specificity is carried almost entirely by the horns; the skull underneath them is a generic rounded wedge with the same oversized white eye as the other two, so if you removed the horns the head would collapse back into the batch.
rows.defect: Three anatomy problems. (1) The near horn is drawn as a closed hoop that crosses in FRONT of the face — it passes over the eye and the ring closes around the muzzle, so it reads as a hoop earring hung on the head rather than a horn rooted at the poll.
