(2) The long flank curtain is rendered as sparse, stiff, straw-colored spikes radiating outward perpendicular to the body outline; it reads as porcupine quills or dried grass. A yak's guard hair is a heavy skirt that hangs straight DOWN under gravity to near the ground, hiding the upper leg entirely. (3) The tail is a fat tapering cylinder with a smooth pale ball stuck on the end, angled down and forward — a mallet, not a bushy horse-like plume — and the legs end bluntly with no cloven hoof read.
rows.fix: Re-root the horns at the top-rear of the skull and sweep them out sideways then up and forward, drawn BEHIND the eye plane so the face is never crossed; leave them open crescents, not closed rings. Replace the radial spike fringe with a gravity-hung curtain: long vertical hair strands starting at the flank line and falling to just above the hoof, dense enough to occlude the upper leg, with a slightly ragged bottom edge. Rebuild the tail as a short bare base with a wide fanned plume of the same long hair. Add split cloven hooves at each foot, dark and slightly wider than the cannon.

rows.readsAs: A zebra — the only one in the batch a stranger would name correctly on sight.
rows.headWhy: Long tapered equine muzzle, straight nasal bridge, a distinct cheek and jaw line, and the eye set high and far back on the skull. It could not be confused with the Wombat or the Wolverine head. The weak point is the ears: they are two dark blobs crowded together at the same point on the poll, forming a single heart-shaped mass, instead of two well-separated tall upright leaf ears.
rows.defect: The species' defining pattern stops at the barrel. The stripes are a dense fan on the torso and a few diagonal slashes on the neck, then the belly, both shoulders below the elbow, all four legs, the rump and the tail are solid blank white — the brief calls for stripes continuing onto legs and belly, and their absence makes the legs read as bare posts. The stripes also radiate as a sunburst from a single point on the flank rather than wrapping the body contour. Second, there is no stiff upright brush mane: the top of the neck is a smooth blank white curve with only a small dark tuft at the poll. Third, the tail is a thin grey stub ending in a smooth grey pebble, reading as a rodent tail, not a tufted tail with a bare upper half. Fourth, the hind legs are straight vertical posts with no hock angulation, so the rear end has no drive.
rows.fix: Continue the striping down all four legs as narrowing horizontal bands that ring the limb and fade toward the hoof, and carry them under the belly and across the rump as chevrons. Re-lay the torso stripes to follow the body's cross-sectional contour — vertical over the barrel, angling back over the haunch — instead of fanning from one origin point. Build the mane as a short erect crest of dark bristles standing perpendicular along the whole neck crest from poll to withers. Rebuild the tail with a bare striped upper half and a long black hair tuft on the lower half. Finally, bend the hind limb: angle the femur forward, drop a defined hock joint behind the body line, and run the cannon vertically to the hoof. Separate the two ears and set them well apart on the poll.

rows.readsAs: a cream-coloured fennec fox standing on deer legs
rows.headWhy: The head is the same construction as the Serval in this batch: small wedge muzzle, one round pale iris with a dark rim, and a pair of big rounded ears fused into a single heart-shaped lobe pinned to the top-centre of the skull. Recolour it tawny and it IS the Serval head. Nothing about it says felid, and nothing says sand cat — the reference asks for a BROAD FLATTENED skull with LOW WIDE-SET ears sitting almost at the sides of the head, and this is a narrow high-domed skull with top-mounted ears.
rows.defect: Three anatomy failures. (1) Limb build is ungulate: four long straight thin stilts of near-equal length with no visible elbow/hock break, ending in small darkened nubs that read as hooves or socks, not paws — no toes, no pad, no furred foot mass. The reference calls for SHORT STOCKY legs. (2) The ears are mounted on top of the cranium and touch each other at the midline, giving a bat-eared-fox skull instead of the low, wide, flattened sand-cat skull. (3) The tail is a thin wire that arcs UP and forward over the croup with a dark band across the middle and a pale end — the reference tail is carried low and straight with a BLACK TIP; here the tip is the lightest part of the tail.
rows.fix: Shorten the legs by ~35% and thicken them, especially the forearm and thigh, so the belly line sits close to the ground and the body reads squat; terminate each leg in a broad rounded paw with 3-4 visible toe bumps and a dark furred sole rather than a tapered nub. Split the ear pair: move each ear outward to the lateral edge of the skull and drop it so its base is level with the eye, then flatten the cranium between them so the skull is wider than it is tall in profile. Straighten the tail to hang low behind the hocks and repaint the banding so the terminal 15% is the darkest value on the animal.

rows.readsAs: a brown dachshund made from a length of pipe
rows.headWhy: Generic. It is the same dome-plus-blunt-snout head as the Seal in this batch, with the same single large white-sclera eye and the same dark blotch behind it; only the hue differs. Swap the two heads and no one could tell. It also fails its own identifying feature — the reference asks for SMALL EXTERNAL EAR FLAPS, the one thing that separates a sea lion from a true seal, and there is no ear flap anywhere on the skull; the dark mark where an ear would be reads as a paint blotch, not a projecting pinna.
rows.defect: The body is a plain extruded cylinder that terminates at the rear in a visible flat circular END CAP — a machined disc with its own rim highlight, sitting where the hindquarters and tail should be. There is no haunch mass, no taper, no tail. All four limbs are identical short cones hanging straight down with rounded tips; there are no flippers of any kind. The reference's defining pose — long fore-flippers propping the chest clear of the ground — is absent, so the chest sits at the same height as the belly and the animal reads as a short-legged terrestrial quadruped.
rows.fix: Replace the cylinder with a fusiform torso: widest just behind the shoulder, tapering continuously to a narrow pelvis, and delete the flat rear cap entirely — cap the volume with a rounded rump plus a short blunt tail between the hind flippers. Swap all four cones for flat paddles: the fore-flippers should be long, wing-shaped and angled outward with the leading edge thick and the trailing edge thin, planted well forward so they lift the sternum and put a clear upward slope into the neck; the hind flippers should be shorter, rotated forward under the pelvis, and fan-shaped rather than conical. Add a small pointed pinna projecting off the skull behind the eye — it is the whole point of this species.

rows.readsAs: a hay bale with legs, or a very shaggy dachshund
rows.headWhy: A small brown dome with a round eye and a slightly upturned snout — the same head as the Sea Lion with a different scale factor. The reference's two head-identifying features are missing: it is not BLUNT and ROUND (it comes to a small point at the nose), and there is no whisker field at all, let alone the dense pale one that defines this animal's face. The head could be swapped with the Sea Lion or the Seal unnoticed.
rows.defect: Two problems. (1) Posture is wrong at the species level: the reference calls for a swimming, belly-up float, and this is a standing terrestrial quadruped on four short cones — no water line, no upturned belly, no rock on the chest, and the hind feet are cones rather than the broad webbed flipper-feet listed. The torso is again a straight cylinder with a flat circular end cap at the rear. (2) The coat is rendered as stiff straight spikes projecting past the silhouette in every direction, evenly spaced and all the same length, which reads as dry straw or a hedgehog's spines rather than the dense wet-looking pelage of an otter. This is not merely a surface issue — the spikes redefine the silhouette.
rows.fix: Rebuild the pose: roll the animal onto its back with the spine as a shallow horizontal curve, belly and chest facing the viewer, forepaws folded on the chest holding a rock, and the hind flippers splayed at the tail end. Replace the cylinder with a thick fusiform body that tapers into a stout muscular tail. Kill the uniform spike fringe — replace with a soft, varied-length fur edge that only breaks the outline in a few places (chest, hip, tail base) and clumps into wet spikes rather than radiating evenly. Blunt the muzzle into a wide flat pad, and add a dense pale whisker mass fanning off it.

rows.readsAs: a grey dog-headed tube standing on four stumpy clawed legs
rows.headWhy: Identical build to the Sea Lion head in this batch — round dome, blunt short snout, one oversized white-sclera eye with a round pupil, a dark blotch behind the eye — differing only in being grey. The reference's own note says the visual test between these two species is the EAR FLAP, and neither head has one, so the two are literally interchangeable here. The muzzle also carries no whiskers.
rows.defect: The reference explicitly warns that propping this animal up on limbs makes it a sea lion, and the render goes further than that: it stands on four legs with clear ground clearance under the belly, and the limbs end in splayed pointed digits that read as CLAWED TOES on a terrestrial foot. There are no flippers. The torso is not a smooth torpedo — it is a straight-sided cylinder with a flat circular end cap at the rear and a hard shoulder crease where the neck joins. Hind flippers trailing straight back, the single most identifying silhouette feature of a true seal, are absent.
rows.fix: Put the belly on the ground. Model the torso as a true fusiform: no straight sides, no end cap, greatest girth at mid-chest, tapering smoothly to the pelvis. Delete the four legs. Give it short fore-flippers pressed close against the ribs, angled back, with five short claws at the tip; and a pair of hind flippers extending straight off the back of the body in line with the spine, fanned open and unable to fold forward. Raise the head and forechest slightly on the elbows to sell the belly-hump posture, and add a whisker fan on the snout.

rows.readsAs: a shaggy mountain goat
rows.headWhy: Specific and not swappable within this batch: a long down-sloping blunt muzzle set on a heavy grizzled skull with a dark facial mask around the eye and pale bosses on the crown. The profile line — flat forehead running into a Roman-nosed muzzle that ends well below the eye line — is unlike any other head here. It genuinely reads caprid.
rows.defect: Two visible defects. (1) The cranial furniture is unreadable: the reference wants SHORT STRAIGHT BACKSWEPT SPIKE HORNS plus LARGE DONKEY-LIKE EARS, and what is rendered is a single ambiguous pale curved pair flanking a dark tuft. Those forms are too short, too pale and too curved to read as horns, and too thick and rigid to read as ears — so the animal has effectively neither, and the two features cancel each other out. (2) There is a hard-edged dark ellipse on the haunch that has no anatomical justification — it reads as a hole punched in the hip or a decal, not as a shadow, because it has no soft edge and does not follow the muscle form. The same disc appears on the Sheep, so it is a shared artifact.
rows.fix: Separate the two features and give each a distinct silhouette: draw the horns as two short, dark, straight cones rising from directly behind the brow and raking BACK along the neck line, keel-ridged and clearly darker than the fur; then place the ears low and outboard of the horns as long, broad, forward-cupped leaves nearly as long as the face, with the inner surface a lighter value so they read as open cups. Remove the dark hip ellipse or replace it with a soft-edged ambient occlusion that wraps the femur and fades out over 20-30px.

rows.readsAs: a spotted fawn or a leopard-print goat kid
rows.headWhy: It is the Sand Cat head at a different colour: same narrow high skull, same small pointed muzzle, same single round eye with a pale iris and dark rim, and the same two rounded ears fused into a single heart-shaped mass on top of the crown. The reference's own words are VERY LARGE UPRIGHT OVAL ears on a SMALL head — these ears are joined at the midline and rounded rather than standing as two separate tall ovals with a gap between them, so even the one feature that should carry the species is generic to this batch.
rows.defect: The feet are the blocker: each of the four legs is a smooth cylinder ending in a slightly darker banded tip with no toes, no pad, no claw — reading as a small hoof or a sock. A cat with hooves. Compounding it, the leg build is ungulate rather than felid: straight columns with no S-curve, no visible hock angle on the hind leg, and no deep chest, so the long legs (correctly long, per the reference) read as a deer's rather than a cat's. The tail is also wrong — it is a thin curled wire tapering to a point, where the reference wants a SHORT, thick, ringed tail.
rows.fix: Terminate every leg in a compact rounded paw with four toe bumps visible in profile and a dark pad edge; keep the metacarpal short so the paw sits flat rather than on tiptoe. Rebuild the hind limb with a real angular hock — a long tibia raking forward, a sharp hock joint, then a near-vertical cannon — so the leg zigzags rather than falling as a straight post, and narrow the ribcage so the body looks small and slung between the legs. Split the ears into two SEPARATE tall upright ovals with clear sky between them, each as tall as the head is long, with the base narrow. Shorten the tail to about a third of its current length and thicken it, with hard black rings and a black tip.

rows.readsAs: a smooth cream-coloured ram or a young goat
rows.headWhy: Distinct within the batch: a narrow pale wedge face angled downward with a heavy scrolled curl of horn wrapping around and below the eye, plus a small dark eye set high. No other head here has the horn scroll or the downturned narrow muzzle, so it could not be swapped with the Serow or anything else in this set.
rows.defect: The single defining feature of the species is missing: THICK WOOLLY FLEECE BLURRING THE BODY OUTLINE. The torso here is a clean smooth capsule with a machined edge and horizontal banding — the outline is the crispest in the batch, the exact opposite of what it should be. Because fleece is a silhouette property, not just a paint property, this is an anatomy/form defect rather than a texture note. Two secondary defects: the SHORT DROOPING TAIL called for in the reference is absent (the rump ends in a bare curve), and the same hard-edged dark ellipse that mars the Serow sits on the haunch here, reading as a hole rather than a shadow.
rows.fix: Give the fleece volume and an irregular boundary: inflate the barrel and shoulder mass by ~15%, then break the outline with overlapping lobes of wool — clumped, uneven, 8-20px deep — all around the back, chest, rump and neck, so no straight or clean-arc segment survives. Hold the crisp edge ONLY where the reference says the animal is bare: the face, the lower legs and the ears, and make that contrast explicit by narrowing the legs where they emerge from the fleece so the wool visibly overhangs them. Add a short thick tail hanging down from the rump and stopping around the hock. Remove or soften the dark hip ellipse.

rows.readsAs: A pale cream lamb or a small white dog with a striped tail glued on — nobody says 'raccoon' without the filename.
rows.headWhy: Generic. Small round cranium, short blunt taper muzzle, one tiny nub ear, and the same large white almond eye with round black pupil + highlight dot that every animal in this batch wears. The only species cue is a single dark smudge around the one visible eye — that is not a bandit mask, it is a bruise. This head is directly interchangeable with the River Otter's; put them side by side and only the tail tells you which is which.
rows.defect: Three failures. (1) Coat value is inverted — the body is near-white/cream where a raccoon is a dark grizzled salt-and-pepper gray-brown; the pale body makes the dark tail rings read as a costume accessory rather than part of the animal. (2) No bandit mask: the mask must be a solid black band running ACROSS the bridge of the nose through both eye sockets, bounded above by a white brow bar and below by a white cheek — here there is only a soft gray blob over the eye. (3) The topline is dead level with the shoulder slightly HIGHER than the rump, which is backwards; the raccoon's signature is a hunched, arched spine with the haunches carried above the shoulders. The tail is also a short upward curl, not the long banded plume carried low and straight behind.
rows.fix: Repaint the coat to a dark grizzled gray-brown (mid-value, not white) and reserve the cream only for the muzzle tip and brow bar. Draw the mask as a hard-edged black band spanning nose-bridge to both temples with a white stripe above and below it, so the mask crosses the face rather than pooling on one eye. Rebuild the spine curve so the hip apex sits ~8-10% above the shoulder apex and the head drops below shoulder level. Lengthen the tail to ~60% of body length, carry it low and straight-back, and put 5-6 alternating black/gray rings on it with a black tip.

rows.readsAs: A small orange pony or a rust-colored deer fawn with a straw broom tied to its rump.
rows.headWhy: Partly specific, but swappable. The black-backed pointed ears and pale narrow muzzle are correct fox cues — and that is exactly the problem, because the Red Panda in this same batch has an identical rust head with dark pointed ears, pale muzzle and the same eye. Swap those two heads and no one notices. Worse, the muzzle here is a straight horizontal peg stuck onto the front of the skull with a visible seam, not a wedge tapering out of the braincase.
rows.defect: The body is built on an ungulate chassis, not a canid one. Legs are long straight columns with the elbow above the belly line and a deep withers hump, giving a shoulder height roughly equal to body length — a fox is low-slung, with body length about twice shoulder height, short legs, and a straight level topline. The brush tail is rendered as radiating straight bristles like a whisk broom rather than a soft mass, and it attaches at the top of the rump and hangs down instead of continuing the line of the spine. Black stockings are absent — the legs are the same orange as the body with only slightly darker feet.
rows.fix: Shorten the legs by roughly 30% and drop the chest so the belly line sits low; flatten the withers hump. Redraw the brush as a single tapering silhouette mass (widest at mid-length, blunt) with fur direction implied inside the shape rather than as individual radiating spikes, and carry it out behind the spine at a shallow angle, keeping the white tip. Add hard-edged black from the carpus/hock down on all four legs so the stockings read as a value break, not a gradient. Fuse the muzzle into the skull — no vertical seam where snout meets face.

rows.readsAs: A small orange fox or a rust-colored dog. It is the Red Fox render with a shorter tail and no white tail-tip.
rows.headWhy: Generic within this batch. Rust head, dark pointed ears, pale short muzzle, same white almond eye with round pupil — that is a description of the Red Fox head above it in this same batch, and the two are genuinely interchangeable. None of the red panda's actual head identity is present: no white face mask, no rust tear-stripes, no white-rimmed round ears, no short blunt bear-like snout.
rows.defect: All three mustReads fail. (1) No white face mask — the face is uniform rust with a slightly paler muzzle; the red panda needs a broad white mask covering the muzzle, cheeks and brows with two vertical rust tear-stripes running from the inner eye down the cheek. (2) Legs and belly are pale peach/orange when they must be jet black — this is the strongest value read on the animal and its absence removes the whole silhouette contrast. (3) The tail is a short dark curl with one band; it must be long (near body length), thick and bushy, held horizontal, with 5-6 alternating pale/rust rings. On top of that the body is on the same long-legged ungulate chassis as the fox, when a red panda is short-legged, plantigrade-ish and cat-sized with an arched back.
rows.fix: This one needs a species-specific rebuild, not a tweak. Paint the mask first: white muzzle/cheeks/brow patch with hard-edged rust tear-stripes below each eye. Flood the legs, feet and entire belly with near-black so the rust reads only on the back, flanks and head. Replace the tail with a long horizontal bushy cylinder carrying alternating pale-cream and rust rings. Shorten and thicken the legs so the belly nearly meets the ground line, round the ears and give them white inner rims, and shorten the muzzle to a blunt bear-like snout so it stops reading as a fox.

rows.readsAs: A pale fallow deer or a young stag — a generic deer with antlers, not specifically a reindeer.
rows.headWhy: The antlers are doing 100% of the work; the skull underneath is generic. Take the antlers off and this cranium — narrow wedge, bulbous pale nose pad, tiny nub ear, big white almond eye with a soft dark surround — is the same skull as the Saiga in this batch. Swap the headgear between those two and nobody would notice the swap happened. The reindeer's own head identity (heavy blunt broad muzzle, big furred nose pad, thick short neck) is missing.
rows.defect: (1) No brow shovel — the antlers are two symmetrical thin twiggy racks sweeping straight up and back, with no forward-projecting palmated brow tine over the face, which is the single feature that separates a reindeer from any other deer. They also read as identical mirrored copies, where real antlers are asymmetric and one brow tine is usually dominant. (2) No neck mane: the neck is a thin smooth tube, where a reindeer carries a thick pale bib of hanging mane along the throat. (3) Hooves are small dark points; reindeer hooves are broad, splayed and rounded — the widest hoof of any deer. (4) Construction problem: the shoulder and haunch masses read as separate pasted-on lobes with visible boundary edges, and there is a distinct gray disc floating on the far hip outline that does not belong to the body form.
rows.fix: Add a wide flattened brow shovel sweeping forward over the muzzle from the base of at least one antler, and break the mirror symmetry between the two racks. Hang a thick pale mane off the underside of the neck from jaw to chest so the throat silhouette bulges downward. Widen and round the hooves to roughly double their current width, splayed with a visible cleft. Blend the shoulder and haunch masses back into the torso solid — soften those boundary edges — and delete or reseat the floating gray hip disc so it reads as the far leg's shoulder rather than a pasted circle.

rows.readsAs: A cartoon gray hippo with two horns taped to its nose — the horns say rhino, everything else says storybook.
rows.headWhy: Specific, thanks to real morphology: two horns rising off the nose tip (correctly nose-mounted, not forehead), a deep boxy jaw, and a much heavier head-to-body ratio than anything else in the batch. This head could not be swapped with any other here. Caveat: the eye is the same oversized white almond with a big round black pupil that every animal in the batch wears, and the reference explicitly calls for a SMALL eye set far back on the side of the skull — the generic eye is the one part of this head that is not species-specific.
rows.defect: (1) The eye is far too large and cartoonish for a rhino, which has a tiny bead eye set low and far back on the cheek; the current eye is the same size as the fox's and sits high and forward. (2) There is a large dark gray disc pasted on the cheek behind the eye that reads as a floating shadow blob, not an ear — the rhino's ears are erect tubular cups on top of the skull and are absent. (3) The hide is completely smooth — no plates, no shoulder/haunch folds, none of the deep armored seams that define a rhino's surface. (4) The tail is a long thin tube ending in a large dark paddle, hanging clear of the body outline; a rhino tail is short, thick at the base, and ends in a flat bristle tassel. (5) Legs are slender columns with small dark points for feet; they must be stumpy pillars ending in a broad flat pad with three visible toenails. (6) The mouth is a thin drawn smile line, which reads as cartoon.
rows.fix: Shrink the eye to roughly a third of its current diameter and move it back and down onto the cheek plane. Delete the dark cheek disc; build two short erect tubular ears on the top-rear of the skull. Cut deep fold seams into the hide — a vertical shoulder fold behind the foreleg, a haunch fold ahead of the hind leg, and a neck fold — so the body reads as plated. Replace the tail with a short thick taper ending in a small flat tassel, held close to the rump. Thicken the legs to pillars and widen the feet into broad pads with three toenails each. Replace the smile line with a squared prehensile or wide-lipped mouth shape depending on the intended species.

rows.readsAs: A pale ferret or a stretched cream-colored weasel on stilts.
rows.headWhy: Generic — and this is the clearest swap case in the batch. The head is a small pale rounded cranium with a blunt short muzzle, a nub ear and the standard white almond eye with round pupil. It is the same head as the Raccoon's in this batch; cover the bodies and you cannot tell them apart. No whiskers, no broad flat nose pad, no low-set eyes-and-nostrils-on-top waterline arrangement that gives an otter its face.
rows.defect: (1) The tail is a thin whip that tapers from a narrow base — an otter's tail is the opposite: very thick and muscular where it meets the rump, occupying nearly the full depth of the hips, then tapering to a point over a length of about 40% of the body. As drawn it reads rat-like. (2) The feet are smooth rounded nubs with no toes and no webbing at all. (3) Coat is pale cream; a river otter is a dark, wet-looking chocolate brown with a paler throat and chin — the value is inverted. (4) The legs are too long and the belly floats well clear of the ground; an otter's body should nearly drag, with the torso a low horizontal tube. (5) No whiskers, which the reference calls for explicitly.
rows.fix: Rebuild the tail so its base is as deep as the hip mass and it tapers in one continuous cone to a point — think a fifth limb, not a string. Re-cut the feet as splayed five-toed paws with webbing filled between the toes. Repaint the coat dark chocolate brown with a cream throat/chin patch only. Drop the belly by shortening the legs about 35% so the torso sits low and horizontal. Add a spray of stiff white whiskers off a broad flat nose pad and set the eye higher on the skull, close to the top line.

rows.readsAs: A pale gazelle or a white antelope. Without the label nobody would say saiga.
rows.headWhy: The ringed horns are the only distinguishing feature and they are an appendage, not the head. The skull beneath them — narrow wedge, tiny nub ear, big white almond eye with a soft dark surround, tapering muzzle with a small dark nose bump — is identical in construction to the Reindeer's in this batch. Swap the horns for antlers and you have the reindeer's head; that is exactly the owner's complaint. Critically, the ONE feature that would have made this head unmistakable is absent.
rows.defect: The bulbous drooping proboscis is missing — this is the diagnostic feature of the entire species and it is not in the picture. What is drawn is a normal straight antelope muzzle that tapers to a point with a slight downward flick at the tip. A saiga's nose is a swollen, inflated, downward-hanging trunk-like snout that overhangs the mouth, with the nostrils pointing at the ground and a visible bulge in profile from the eye forward. Secondary: the horns are correct in being straight, upright and ringed, but they are set too far back on the crown and lean rearward — saiga horns rise nearly vertically from directly above the eyes.
rows.fix: Rebuild the muzzle from the eye forward: swell the nasal region into a rounded bulbous mass roughly 1.5x the depth of the lower jaw, curve its front profile convexly downward so the nose tip hangs below the mouth line, and put two large downward-facing nostril openings at the bottom of that bulge. The profile silhouette must read as a hump-and-droop, not a straight wedge. Move the horn bases forward so they sit directly over the eye sockets and stand them near-vertical with only a slight backward lean, keeping the amber translucent ringing.

rows.readsAs: A tan big-cat toy with a rectangular patch of black scribble glued to its ribs — a lion wearing a barcode, or a cat that walked through burnt grass
rows.headWhy: Specific: the only round-topped ear in the batch, a large amber round-pupil eye set forward on a short blunt feline muzzle, plus stripe marks carried up onto the cheek and brow. Nothing else here could wear it. Weak point is the muzzle — it is a soft rounded knob with no nose leather or whisker bed, so the head is carried by ear+eye alone.
rows.defect: The stripe field is a floating slab, not a coat pattern. It occupies a rectangle over the mid-torso with a HARD STRAIGHT horizontal top edge along the spine and a hard vertical stop at the shoulder and hip; the strokes hang straight down past the belly line as loose bristles, so they read as grass or hair pasted over the body rather than pigment in the fur. Shoulder, haunch, all four legs and the entire tail are blank orange — a tiger is striped to the toes and the tail is ringed to a black tip. There is also no white cheek ruff or white eyebrow spot, and the feet terminate in blunt rounded blocks with no toe split, so a paw reads as a hoof.
rows.fix: Drive the stripes off a body-space UV rather than a screen-space rect: sample the torso surface normal so each stripe wraps the barrel and shortens/curves as it approaches the belly and back silhouette, and clip every stroke to the body path so nothing hangs off it. Continue the same field onto shoulder, haunch and upper legs at reduced width, and replace the tail with 5-6 discrete dark bands ending in a solid black tip. Add the white cheek ruff wedge below the eye and a white brow patch above it, and split the front feet into 3-4 visible toe lobes with a darker pad shadow.

rows.readsAs: A pink dachshund or mole with two ivory fangs — a burrowing animal, not a marine one
rows.headWhy: Specific only because of the tusk pair. Strip those and you have the same rounded muzzle box the Warthog and Boar wear, with a big cartoon eye. There is no walrus-specific structure: no squared bristle pad, no whiskers, no heavy fatty brow, and the eye is a large white-sclera anime eye rather than the small dark bead the sheet calls for.
rows.defect: Two family-level errors. (1) The limbs are not flippers — both front and rear end in three splayed CLAWED toes, a digging/mustelid foot, and the front limb has a distinct upper-arm and wrist rather than the single flat paddle a pinniped has. (2) The mustRead bristle moustache is entirely absent: the muzzle is a plain rounded mass with one dark round nose disc, no vibrissae field at all, which is the single most identifying feature of the animal. Separately there is a construction fault at the head/neck junction — a right-angle notch is bitten out of the silhouette under the jaw where the head solid and the body solid fail to union, leaving a visible step and a second one at the crown.
rows.fix: Swap this family to the flipper foot: front limb becomes a short broad triangular paddle with 4-5 shallow nail notches along the trailing edge and no visible wrist; rear becomes a single fused fan splayed sideways behind the body. Build the moustache as a squared-off pad protruding forward of the nose with 20-30 short radiating bristle strokes clipped to that pad, and drop the tusks from BEHIND that pad so they pass in front of the chest. Shrink the eye to roughly a third of its current diameter, kill the white sclera, and set it deep in a fleshy fold. Fix the boolean so head and torso union into one silhouette with a fatty roll instead of a notch.

rows.readsAs: A small hornless rhino or a tapir calf — the tusks read as two nose horns
rows.headWhy: This head and the Wild Boar's are the SAME head: same rounded wedge box, same small dark forward-pointed ear in the same spot, same eye at the same height, same dark disc snout, same pair of straight white spikes at the same angle. Cover the bodies and nobody could tell which render is which — this is the owner's complaint reproduced literally inside one batch.
rows.defect: Three mustRead items missing or wrong. There is no erect bristly mane — the neck and spine are perfectly smooth, which is the feature that separates a warthog silhouette from any other pig. There are no facial warts. The tail hangs DOWN as a thick club curving forward under the rump, when the defining warthog pose is a thin tail carried bolt upright with a terminal tuft. The tusks also sprout from the top of the muzzle like rhino horns as straight spikes, instead of curving up and outward from the jawline outside the lips, and the head is a rounded box rather than the flat-fronted wedge the note asks for.
rows.fix: Add a dorsal bristle crest as a distinct spiky ridge running crown-to-shoulder-to-mid-spine, tallest at the nape. Flip the tail to vertical: a thin straight stalk rising above the back line with a dark tuft at the tip. Move the tusk roots down to the jawline and give them a real outward curve (root near the mouth corner, sweeping up and away from the face) so they silhouette against the cheek. Flatten the front of the skull into a broad vertical facial disc and hang two paired wart lobes on it, one under the eye and one mid-muzzle. Every one of these also breaks the head-share with the Boar.

rows.readsAs: A grey bighorn sheep or an ibex — the horn curl, not the body, is what a stranger names
rows.headWhy: The skull itself is the same rounded grey box with the same small dark pointed ears the Warthog and Boar wear; all identity is in a detachable horn prop. Worse, the horn overlaps and OCCLUDES the face, so the eye, the brow and the broad wet muzzle the mustRead calls for are not legible at all — there is nothing head-specific left to recognise.
rows.defect: The horns are the wrong species. They are a tight pale ram curl that spirals down, forward and inward across the cheek, ending in front of the muzzle and drawing a closed ring over the face. A water buffalo's horns are a wide flat crescent that sweeps BACK and OUTWARD from the poll, low and nearly horizontal, thick and triangular in section, tips turning up behind the head — they must never cross the face. The body also undersells the animal: back is straight but the chest is shallow and the neck is slim, so there is no heavy low-slung mass, and the head is carried level rather than dropped low.
rows.fix: Rebuild the horn as a back-swept crescent: root wide on the poll, run outward and rearward past the ear, taper to an upturned tip behind the shoulder line, with a triangular cross-section and ridged growth rings — and z-order it BEHIND the head so the face is never crossed. With the face uncovered, give it the buffalo-specific muzzle: a broad flat wet-black nose pad much wider than the skull is deep, big open nostrils, held low near knee height on a thick dewlapped neck. Deepen the chest and drop the belly line to put mass under the animal.

rows.readsAs: A wooden pull-toy dachshund — a tube on four cut dowels
rows.headWhy: Unique in this batch purely by scale and by the tapered mustelid muzzle with a small rounded ear set low and far back. But it is thin identity: at render size the eye is a dot with no readable iris or pupil, and the head is a smooth cone that would serve equally as an otter, ferret or mongoose.
rows.defect: The limbs and the tail are all the same object — four short truncated cylinders plus one horizontal truncated cylinder at the rear, every one of them ending in a flat elliptical CUT CAP with a lighter interior, so they read as sawn-off dowels or hollow pipe. There are no feet at all: no pads, no toes, no ground contact shaping. The tail is the worst case — same diameter as a leg, dead straight, dead horizontal, flat-ended, no taper, no fur, no dark tip, so it cannot be told from a fifth limb. The body is also not the aspect the sheet asks for (reads roughly 2.5:1, not 4:1) and is a straight rigid tube with no arch through the spine.
rows.fix: Cap every limb with an actual foot: a small five-toe pad splayed on the ground plane, toes visible, and remove the flat end ellipse so no limb shows an open section. Rebuild the tail as a separate tapered form — thicker at the base than the legs, narrowing over its length, held in a slight upward S, with a fur outline and a darker tip. Lengthen the torso by roughly half again and put a real arch in it (hump at mid-spine, dip at the shoulders) so the animal reads as bounding rather than as a plank.

rows.readsAs: A donkey or onager — correctly named at a glance, though the long thin face pulls it toward a llama
rows.headWhy: Specific: the tall dark-backed leaf ears are unlike anything else in the batch and cannot be transplanted, and the long tapering equine muzzle with a small nostril line and a high-set eye is genuinely a horse-family skull rather than the shared box.
rows.defect: Two things. (1) The ears are drawn as a mirrored symmetric pair fanning outward from a single point at the crown, both shown in full frontal spread on a head that is in pure profile — the result is a heart/butterfly shape stuck on the skull, a projection error rather than a shape error. (2) The mustRead erect mane is missing: the crest of the neck is smooth and the same pale cream as the flank, when the stiff upright black mane from poll to withers is a primary onager identifier. Minor third: the flank carries two lighter oval blobs over shoulder and haunch that stop at a soft edge and read as pasted-on patches rather than as muscle shading.
rows.fix: Put the ears in profile — near ear drawn full and upright with its dark inner surface visible, far ear offset behind it, narrower and darker, with the two roots separated across the width of the poll instead of meeting at one point. Add a short erect mane as a hard-edged dark brush along the top of the neck standing above the neckline, plus a matching dark dorsal stripe to the tail. Blend the shoulder and haunch ovals into the coat gradient so the mass reads as underlying muscle, not a decal.

rows.readsAs: A straw-covered piñata pig, or the Warthog render with a shaggy coat added
rows.headWhy: Identical to the Warthog's head — same wedge box, same dark forward ear in the same position, same eye, same snout disc, same pair of straight white spikes at the same angle out of the top of the muzzle. The two heads are directly interchangeable, which is exactly the standing complaint.
rows.defect: The bristles are applied as a uniform halo around the ENTIRE torso outline — top, sides, chest and belly — hanging below the gut like a grass skirt and radiating outward at every angle, so the coat reads as attached straw rather than as hair lying along the body. The mustRead dorsal mane is therefore invisible: there is no crest, because the bristles are everywhere equally. The silhouette also misses the boar's defining proportion — the back is level from shoulder to rump with the highest point at mid-spine, instead of a tall shoulder hump sloping down to a low rump, so there is no front-heavy wedge. Tusks repeat the Warthog error: straight spikes out of the top of the snout instead of curving up from the lower jaw.
rows.fix: Restrict long bristles to a dorsal crest (crown → nape → mid-spine, tallest over the withers) and let the flank hair lie down along the body direction, short and swept back, clipped to the silhouette so nothing dangles below the belly. Raise the shoulder/withers mass well above the hip and slope the spine downward to the rump so the wedge reads even in pure silhouette. Re-root the tusks at the lower jaw with a genuine outward-then-upward curve, and shorten the upper pair to small nubs. Then differentiate the skull from the Warthog: longer straighter snout, smaller eye set further back, ear tufted rather than bare.

rows.readsAs: a striped pony or a small okapi standing square
rows.headWhy: Specific within the batch — it is the only long tapering wedge muzzle, and the dark bars running across the cheek and down the bridge belong to nothing else here. But it is distinctive in the wrong direction: the muzzle is a thin equine cone where a hyena needs a deep, heavy, blunt box of a muzzle, and the two large rounded ears are set touching each other on the centre-top of the skull, which reads rabbit, not the wide-set pointed ears of the reference.
rows.defect: The defining read is missing entirely. The topline runs level and if anything rises toward the rump — front and hind legs are the same length and the shoulder carries no extra height, so there is no slope. The erect spinal crest is also misplaced: the long bristles radiate off the TAIL as a spiky halo, while the spine itself carries only flat painted stripes. The tail attaches high on the mid-back, well forward of the hindquarters, as a pale club sitting on top of the loin rather than hanging from the rump.
rows.fix: Raise the shoulder mass and lengthen the forelegs by roughly 15% over the hind, then drop the hip so the topline falls in one continuous line from withers to croup. Move the bristle field off the tail and onto the spine as an erect crest running withers-to-croup, keeping it above the silhouette. Reattach the tail at the actual rump behind the hind leg. Shorten the muzzle by about a third and deepen the jaw so the head is a wedge in plan but a heavy block in profile, and move the two ears apart to sit above the outer corners of the skull.

rows.readsAs: a tiny white goat or pony foal, drawn at about a fifth of the frame
rows.headWhy: Generic. At the size it renders the head is a pale nub carrying the same kit as the hyena — a pair of small rounded ears set close together on the crown and one round eye with a ring iris. Strip the colour and it could be swapped with the Tahr's or the hyena's and nobody would flag it. There is no dark facial stripe to the nose, and the eyes are neither huge nor black, so the single strongest identifying mark of the animal is absent.
rows.defect: This is not a glider. Posture is a four-square standing quadruped on four stiff pale legs with hoof-like tips, not a spread airborne pose. There is no patagium anywhere — no membrane between wrist and ankle, no stretched skin edge, nothing connecting fore and hind limb. The tail is a short bristled fan at the hip, not a long bushy tail matching the body length. The whole organism also occupies only a small central patch of the 440px frame, so it is tiny and unreadable next to every other card in the batch.
rows.fix: Switch this to the gliding build: splay all four limbs outward and draw the membrane as a continuous skin sheet spanning wrist to ankle on each side, with a soft scalloped trailing edge so the silhouette is a rectangle, not a barrel on legs. Replace the hoof tips with small grasping paws. Redraw the tail as a long cylindrical bushy rope at least as long as the trunk. Enlarge the eyes to the prominent setting the row asks for, fill them near-black, and run a dark dorsal stripe from between the ears down the bridge to the nose. Scale the whole organism up to fill the frame like the rest of the batch.

rows.readsAs: a grey sheep or a hornless goat with a dark head
rows.headWhy: This is the clearest instance of the standing complaint in the batch, and it is provable rather than impressionistic: the head is the same asset as the Tasmanian Devil's. Both are a dark rounded skull with one large flat dark disc for an ear pasted on the upper side, the same white-ringed round eye with an amber iris in the same position, the same short muzzle curving downward, and the same small nose bump on the side of the tip. Swap the two crops and no one could tell. Nothing about it says bear — the down-curving snout with the disc ear reads closer to a seal.
rows.defect: No bear anatomy survives. The body is a smooth grey barrel with a level topline standing on four thin cylindrical sticks that terminate in tiny dark two-toe nubs — cloven-hoof feet on a bear. There are no long curved climbing claws and no broad flat plantigrade soles. The coat is mid-grey, not jet black, and the golden-cream chest crescent is absent. The tail is a flat matte black circle stamped onto the rear hip, which reads as a hole punched through the flank rather than a tail.
rows.fix: Rebuild the limbs on the plantigrade type: thick columnar legs with a visible heel, a broad flat sole planted along its full length, and five long curved claws projecting past the toe line at each foot. Drop the belly and round the shoulder hump so the torso is heavy and loose-skinned rather than a smooth tube. Recolour the coat to near-black with a sheen and paint a large cream crescent across the chest. Kill the flat disc tail and give the rump a small tuft or nothing at all. Most importantly, differentiate the head from the Tasmanian Devil's: a bear skull wants a broad forehead, small round ears set wide on the corners of the crown, and a short straight muzzle that does not curve downward.

rows.readsAs: a bighorn sheep or a young ram
rows.headWhy: Specific by virtue of the horns — it is the only head in the batch carrying a heavy pale curl, so it could not be swapped. But the horn is doing all the work and doing it wrong: it is drawn as a flat cream ribbon sweeping forward and down around the cheek in a bighorn spiral, and it passes IN FRONT of the eye, occluding it completely. The face underneath has no visible eye at all, so the head has no gaze.
rows.defect: Two anatomy problems. First the horn: it is a flat constant-width band with no taper, no ridging and no root, it curls forward into a ram spiral instead of the short thick backward-and-down curve the reference calls for, and it is layered over the eye so the eye is lost. Second, the tail is the same flat brown disc stamped on the rear hip seen on the Sun Bear, Takin and Tapir — a circle sitting on the flank, reading as a hole. The shaggy mane also renders as stiff straw-coloured spikes radiating clear off the silhouette rather than as hair hanging down over the neck and shoulders.
rows.fix: Shorten the horns to roughly half their current length, taper them from a thick root to a point, add transverse ridging, and re-sweep them backward and downward behind the ear so they clear the eye socket entirely. Draw them at a darker value than the face so they read as keratin. Restore the eye with its iris and horizontal bar pupil, set high and lateral on the skull as a goat's is. Replace the disc tail with a short tapering flap. Convert the mane from radiating spikes to layered strands that follow gravity, hanging down past the shoulder line rather than sticking out sideways.

rows.readsAs: a shaggy cream goat, or a straw-covered sheep
rows.headWhy: Distinguishable, just barely, on the strength of the muzzle: it is the only heavy arched Roman nose in the batch and the jaw is squarer and deeper than the Tahr's or the Tapir's, so a swap would be noticed. But the two features that should carry the identity both fail — the horns are painted in nearly the same cream as the coat and read as a smudge rather than horn, and the eye is a flat dark almond blot with a single white sliver, carrying no iris and no pupil at all. It looks like a closed or missing eye.
rows.defect: The horns are present in geometry but invisible in value — same cream tone as the surrounding face, no outline, no shadow, so at a glance the animal reads as hornless and the wildebeest sweep the reference demands never registers. The eye has no iris or pupil structure. The shaggy coat is rendered as hundreds of stiff straw-yellow spikes radiating perpendicular off the entire body outline, which reads as a bale of hay rather than long hanging hair. The tail is again the flat brown disc on the rear hip. The humped shoulder is also under-built — the topline is nearly flat where the reference wants a distinct withers hump.
rows.fix: Recolour the horns to a dark grey-brown two or three values below the coat, add a cast shadow where they meet the skull, and re-sweep them outward from the crown then sharply back so the wildebeest curve is legible in silhouette. Give the eye a real iris and a horizontal bar pupil. Reangle the coat strands to lie along the body and hang downward under gravity, with the longest fringe on the throat, brisket and belly, instead of firing outward on all sides. Raise the shoulder into a real hump so the topline drops from withers to hip. Remove the disc tail.

rows.readsAs: a grey domestic pig or a peccary
rows.headWhy: Unswappable, because the big pink disc snout with two drilled nostril holes appears nowhere else in the batch. But it is unique as the wrong animal — the reference explicitly says this must be a short mobile proboscis and NOT a flat disc snout, and the render delivers exactly the flat disc snout it warns against. The ears compound it: they are two small dark triangular slashes cut into the side of the skull, reading as gashes rather than the upright oval ears a tapir carries.
rows.defect: The single defining feature is inverted into the pig read the reference forbids — a flat circular pink pad on the front of the face instead of a proboscis hanging past the lower lip. The rump is wrong too: the back is essentially level and the hindquarters are no higher or rounder than the shoulder, so the sloping-back, high-rump profile is absent. Feet are small dark two-toe cloven nubs, but a tapir is odd-toed, with three toes behind and four in front on broad splayed pads. The tail is the same flat black disc stamped on the hip as on the Sun Bear, Tahr and Takin. The torso is also the identical smooth ribbed grey barrel used for the Sun Bear and Tasmanian Devil.
rows.fix: Delete the pink disc. Extend the upper lip and nose forward and DOWNWARD into a short flexible trunk that overhangs the mouth, tapering to a small nostril pair at the tip, with a visible crease where it leaves the skull so it reads as mobile flesh. Raise and round the rump above the shoulder and let the back dip between them. Replace the cloven nubs with broad splayed multi-toed pads — three toes on the hind, four on the front. Replace the disc tail with a short conical nub. Swap the triangular ear slashes for upright rounded ovals with pale rims set on top of the skull, and give the torso its own mass so it stops sharing a silhouette with the bear.

rows.readsAs: a small grey lamb or a donkey foal with a dark head
rows.headWhy: It is the Sun Bear's head. Identical dark rounded skull, identical large flat dark disc ear on the upper side, identical white-ringed round eye with amber iris at the same placement, identical short down-curving muzzle with the same small nose bump at the tip. Placed side by side the two crops are interchangeable. Worse, it is the opposite of what this animal needs: the head here is SMALLER than the body proportion suggests, where the devil's defining feature is a head oversized and blocky relative to the trunk, with a wide gaping jaw. There is no gape, no jaw line, no teeth.
rows.defect: Almost nothing from the reference row is present. The head is small and rounded rather than oversized and blocky, and the jaws are closed and featureless rather than gaping. The coat is mid-grey, not black, and the white chest band is entirely absent. The tail is a thin curved hook sticking out and up from the rump, where the reference calls for a thick short tapering tail nearly as fat as the hind leg at its root. The legs are the same thin cylindrical sticks as the Sun Bear and Tapir, so the low stocky build never reads. The torso is the same ribbed grey barrel used for both of those animals.
rows.fix: Enlarge the head to roughly a third of the body length and rebuild it as a broad wedge — wide at the cheeks and zygomatic arches, tapering to a short blunt snout — then open the jaw to a wide gape with the lower jaw dropped and a red mouth interior and visible canines. Set the ears as short rounded flaps with pink inner skin on the back corners of the skull, replacing the flat disc. Recolour the coat to black and paint a broad white crescent band across the chest and a second across the rump. Thicken the tail into a short cone, fat at the base and tapering to a blunt tip, carried low. Shorten and thicken all four legs and lower the belly so the animal sits close to the ground. This head must not share geometry with the Sun Bear.

rows.readsAs: A pale dun cartoon pony with a straw broom stuck to its rump
rows.headWhy: This head is the batch's default head. Cropped and enlarged, it is construction-identical to Wild Pony and Wolf: the same pair of overlapping rounded ear lobes forming a heart at the same skull position, the same smooth tapered wedge muzzle with a blunt squared-off nose tip, the same single short curved slit mouth line, the same round glossy eye with a white sclera ring. Only the fill colour and iris hue differ. Swap it onto the Wolf and nobody would see it.
rows.defect: The stiff erect neck mane is entirely missing — there is no bristle mass anywhere on the crest from poll to withers, which is the single feature that separates a Przewalski horse from a generic equine. The only bristle mass in the picture is on the RUMP, where a fan of stiff spikes plus a separate pale tapered stub stand in for the tail; the tail root sits high on the back forward of the croup, and the pale stub overlaps the spike fan so it reads as a second appendage rather than a tail. Legs are perfectly straight cylinders — no stifle, no hock angulation, no elbow — so the hind limb has no drive. The haunch is a soft applied oval rather than mass in the torso solid.
rows.fix: Move the bristle emitter from the croup to the neck crest: a 12-15px tall brush running poll-to-withers, hairs perpendicular to the crest line, no forelock. Rebuild the tail as a single mass springing from the point of the croup and hanging down past the hock — dock at the top, hair below — and delete the pale stub. Break the hind limb at the stifle and hock so the cannon is vertical and the gaskin slopes forward. For the head: give the horse a long narrow leaf ear angled outward, a pronounced cheekbone/jowl at the jaw angle, and a convex nasal bone with a squared muzzle plane — none of which the wolf or pony should share.

rows.readsAs: A capybara, or a shorn sheep that borrowed a pig's nose
rows.headWhy: The truncated snout ending in a pink disc with two dark nostrils is loud and unshared — no other head in this batch has it, so the swap test passes. But everything behind the disc is the shared default: the same heart-shaped double ear lobe and the same round white-ringed eye as the horse and wolf.
rows.defect: The snout is short and blunt, roughly one third of the head, where the row calls for a long wedge — the disc is pushed onto a rounded muzzle rather than terminating a long tapering face. No tusks at all; the mouth is a plain dark line with nothing emerging from the lower jaw. The high shoulder hump is absent — the topline runs dead level from withers to croup, so the animal has no forequarter mass. The bristly crest has been emitted as a fringe along the flanks and the belly line rather than standing up along the spine, which puts the boar's signature hair in the one place a boar does not have it.
rows.fix: Lengthen the face so the snout is half the head length and taper it in plan so the disc caps a wedge, not a ball. Add two short ivory tusks curving up out of the lower jaw at the mouth corner. Raise the withers into a real hump 15-20% above the croup and slope the back down to the rear. Move the bristle emitter from the flank/ventral outline to the dorsal crest, nape to mid-back, with the longest hairs over the hump.

rows.readsAs: The Wild Horse again, after being rolled in straw
rows.headWhy: Interchangeable with Wild Horse — same heart ear lobes at the same coordinates, same wedge muzzle, same slit mouth, same eye, same colour family. The only difference is straw spikes near the jaw. A stranger shown the two heads side by side would call them the same animal.
rows.defect: Two failures. First, the shaggy mane and forelock the row demands do not exist as a mane: the shag is a scatter of loose straw-coloured spikes strewn over the whole torso silhouette — flank, belly, shoulder, rump — reading as debris stuck to the coat rather than hair growing from a crest, and no hair falls over the eyes. Second, the pony proportions are not there — leg length, barrel depth and body length are the same as the Wild Horse in this batch, so the two silhouettes are the same animal at the same scale. The rump tail is the same misplaced spike-fan-plus-pale-stub as the horse.
rows.fix: Kill the whole-body spike scatter. Emit a single dense mane along the crest that falls to ONE side of the neck, plus a forelock hank that hangs forward over the brow and breaks the eye. Then re-proportion: shorten the leg column ~25% and deepen the barrel ~15% so the belly drops below the elbow and the silhouette reads long and low against the horse. Give the pony a shorter, broader forehead and a smaller muzzle so the head differs from the horse at a glance.

rows.readsAs: A white domestic sheep with a fat tan ring stuck on its face
rows.headWhy: The horn ring makes it unmistakable in this batch, so it passes the swap test — but it passes for the wrong reason: the identifying shape is a misplaced prop, not skull architecture. The underlying head is a plain pale capsule with a small dark almond eye and no ear at all.
rows.defect: The horn is placed wrong and reads as an object lying on top of the face. It is a flat open ring centred over the cheek and MUZZLE, covering the nose bridge and crossing the mouth, with no visible root on the skull. A ram's horn springs from a boss on top of the skull behind the eye, sweeps back and down behind the jaw, then curls forward below the ear — it never crosses the muzzle. Only the near horn is drawn; there is no far-side horn peeking past the skull, so the head reads as one-sided. The horn is a smooth flat tan band with no annular growth ridges and no taper from base to tip. The ear is entirely missing. The coat also contradicts the row: it reads as woolly fleece fringe rather than short coarse hair, which is exactly the domestic sheep the note warns against.
rows.fix: Re-root the horn: origin above and behind the eye on the skull top, first arc sweeping back and down past the ear, second arc curling forward and out to end level with the jaw, tip clear of the muzzle. Draw the far horn as a partially occluded duplicate offset behind the skull. Add 8-12 transverse growth ridges along the outer curve and taper the section to a blunt point. Add a short pointed ear tucked under the horn base. Replace the fleece fringe with a short flat hair coat so the body outline is clean and muscular, and add a dark saddle/rump patch typical of argali.

rows.readsAs: A striped fawn or a thylacine — a small hoofed animal with tiger stripes
rows.headWhy: Unique by accident: the vertical amber slit pupil and the flat round ear DISC lying against the side of the skull are unlike anything else here, so it could not be swapped unnoticed. But the specificity is wrong specificity — it is a long pointed lizard/mongoose wedge, not a cat skull, and the round side-mounted disc is not a cat ear.
rows.defect: Nothing below the eye is feline. The head is a long narrow wedge with a downturned pointed nose tip and no cheek mass, no short square muzzle, no whisker pad, and the ear is a flat disc pasted on the SIDE of the skull instead of an erect pointed triangle rising off the top. All four legs are dead-straight cylinders sawn off flat at the ground with a slightly darker elliptical cap — no paw, no toes, no pad, no claw; the front feet are identical to the Wolf's, so the promised per-family foot never rendered. The limbs have no carpus, hock or shoulder, so the digitigrade cat stance is absent and the topline is a flat ungulate back with no shoulder-blade rise or loin dip. The tail is a thick smooth club with one dark blotch and a pale rounded end, not a thick tail with dark rings and a black tip.
rows.fix: Rebuild the skull: short broad cranium, muzzle no more than a third of head length ending in a blunt nose leather, prominent cheek/whisker pad, and two erect pointed triangular ears rising off the top of the skull with the eye set well forward for binocular placement. Keep the slit pupil. Replace both foot caps with an actual paw — a rounded pad silhouette with three visible toe bumps at the front, forefoot wider than hind. Bend the limbs: hock high and angled on the hind, wrist stepped on the fore. Redraw the tail as a straight thick cylinder with 4-5 evenly spaced dark rings and a solid black tip, and lift the shoulder blade so the back has a feline dip behind the withers.

rows.readsAs: A grey striped horse with a pale ribbon draped over its face
rows.headWhy: The pale hooked shapes across the face make it unswappable in this batch, but only as a graphic — the head itself is a featureless blunt grey capsule with NO eye drawn at all and no jaw, cheek or muzzle definition, so the identity is carried entirely by an overlay that is in the wrong place.
rows.defect: The horns read as two flat pale crescents floating on top of the picture, not as horn growing from bone. One sits on the crown, the second is draped across the MUZZLE below the nose bridge, and neither shows a base or boss where it meets the skull, so the pair reads as a ring tossed over the face. There is no eye anywhere on the head. The chin beard is completely absent and the neck mane is absent from the crest — instead a large dark bristle patch has been dumped on the mid-flank and shoulder, far from any crest. The skull is a rounded capsule where the row calls for a heavy boxy cow head with a broad square muzzle. The topline is level: no high withers dropping away to the rump. The tail is again the shared pale stub plus spike fan mounted high on the back.
rows.fix: Rebuild the horns as one solid mass: a thick rugose boss across the top of the skull, then smooth horn sweeping down and OUT to the side before hooking sharply up and inward, tips above the crown, both horns visible with the far one occluded by the skull. Nothing crosses the muzzle. Square off the muzzle into a broad flat nose plane and deepen the jaw so the head is boxy in profile. Add a dark eye with a horizontal bar pupil set high and far back on the skull. Move the bristle emitter to two correct places — an upright mane from poll to withers, and a long hanging beard under the chin and throat. Raise the withers well above the croup and slope the back down. Replace the rump spike fan with a long thin tail ending in a black hair switch at the hock.

rows.readsAs: A grey pony or a young donkey — not a canid at all
rows.headWhy: It is the Wild Horse head recoloured grey with an amber iris. Enlarged side by side the two are the same drawing: the same overlapping heart-shaped ear lobes at the same skull coordinate, the same smooth tapered wedge muzzle with a squared blunt tip, the same short curved mouth slit, the same round eye with a pale ring. There is no wolf skull anywhere in this image.
rows.defect: Head, limbs and tail are all the equine defaults. The muzzle is a long thin cone with no stop, no cheek mass, no jaw depth, and the ears are rounded overlapping blobs rather than erect triangles — the row's single most important call. The neck is a long slender horse neck attached with a visible seam band, with no ruff and no scruff mass at the shoulder. All four legs are straight tubes ending in a flat-cut cylinder with a darker elliptical cap — identical to the Wildcat's, so there is no paw, no toe, no pad and no claw on a species whose whole silhouette depends on the foot. There is no hock bend, no deep narrow chest, and no tuck-up at the loin. The tail is the shared pale tapered stub plus a spike fan mounted high on the rump, so it juts backward off the spine instead of hanging as a bushy brush from the croup.
rows.fix: Replace the skull wholesale: broad flat cranium, clear stop at the brow, a shorter deep muzzle with a wide black nose leather and heavy lower jaw, plus two erect triangular ears set wide on the top of the skull with visible inner-ear cavity. Widen the neck and add a cheek/throat ruff. Rebuild the feet as compact oval paws with four toe bumps and short blunt claws, forefoot larger than hind. Angle the hind limb at the hock and narrow the chest in plan while deepening it in profile, with a clear tuck-up behind the ribs. Delete the stub-and-fan tail and draw a single bushy cylinder hanging from the croup, widest at mid-length, tapering to a dark tip, carried level or low and never curled.

rows.readsAs: a bone-white piglet with rabbit ears and an anteater's snout
rows.headWhy: The tall paired ears and tubular snout are the right IDEA, but the ear is the same two-leaf token used on the African Wild Dog and the Armadillo — the Armadillo head is literally a smaller recolour of this one. Swap the two and nobody would notice. The snout is a flat parallel-sided plank with a dot nose, a straight seam for a mouth and no lower jaw, so it carries no species information either.
rows.defect: Three anatomy misses. (a) The tail is a thin upward-curling whip of even width — the reference (and the animal) want a thick kangaroo-like tail as deep as the thigh at the root, tapering over its length. (b) The feet are dark oval caps on cylinder ends, reading as small hooves; an aardvark's whole identity below the knee is huge shovel claws on the forefeet. (c) The snout has no taper and no nostril disc — it is a rectangle stuck to the face, and the ear bases overlap the eye so the skull has no cheek.
rows.fix: Rebuild the tail as a cone: root width ≈ 0.9x the thigh, tapering to a point past the hocks, carried low with a slight downward arc. Replace the hoof caps on the forelimbs with 3-4 splayed heavy claws (short, blunt, ground-contacting) and give the hind foot a longer plantigrade sole. Taper the snout ~25% from base to tip, curve the top line down over the last third, add a nostril pad wider than the snout tip, and move the ear roots back and up behind the eye so a cheek plane is visible.

rows.readsAs: an elephant — unmistakable
rows.headWhy: The ground-reaching trunk, the paired curved tusks and the trunk-over-tusk overlap make this head impossible to confuse with anything else in the batch. It is the only head here that carries real species information. What weakens it: the eye is an oversized round cartoon eye with a big white catchlight set high on the forehead, where an elephant's is small, low, heavy-lidded and set just above the tusk line.
rows.defect: (a) The ear is a hard-edged dark RECTANGLE with a straight vertical leading edge — no lobe, no dorsal fold, no notch — and it is scaled so large it covers the shoulder and half the ribcage, so it reads as a saddle blanket draped over the body rather than an ear on the skull. (b) The tail ends in an enormous solid dark OVAL, wider than the tail is thick, which reads as a spoon or paddle. (c) The trunk meets the face as a cylinder with a visible flat end-cap disc, and a loose grey sausage-stroke crosses the cheek with nothing to attach to.
rows.fix: Shrink the ear to roughly head height (top edge at the skull dome, bottom edge no lower than the shoulder joint), anchor its front edge to the skull just behind the eye, fold the top corner forward, and cut the trailing edge as a soft lobed curve rather than a straight line. Tint it in body grey with a fanned vein pattern instead of a uniform dark slab. Replace the tail oval with a thin wisp brush of 5-8 hairs no wider than the tail. Blend the trunk root into the brow with a continuous surface (kill the cap disc) and delete or reroute the cheek stroke into a real jaw/lip line.

rows.readsAs: a blotchy fawn or young deer with a brush tail
rows.headWhy: This head is the Aardvark's head in tan. Identical two-leaf pointed ear pair, identical thin plank muzzle with a dot nose and a straight mouth seam. The species' single most recognisable feature — huge ROUND satellite-dish ears as broad as they are tall — is absent, and the black muzzle mask is absent. Swap this head onto the Aardvark and nothing would look wrong.
rows.defect: Two blockers. (1) NO FEET. Every leg is a smooth tapering cylinder that simply stops flat at ground level — no paw, no toes, no pad, no claws. On a cursorial carnivore this is the most-read part of the silhouette. (2) The ears are tall pointed leaves; the animal requires broad round ears. Combined with the very fine ungulate legs and the thin snout, the picture reads as a deer, not a canid.
rows.fix: Give all four limbs a digitigrade paw: a compact oval pad platform angled forward, 4 visible toes with short blunt claws, and a raised wrist/hock so the leg breaks at the pastern instead of running straight to the floor. Replace the ear with a broad rounded disc — width ≈ 1.1x height, ≈ 0.5x skull length, set high and outward on the crown, dark on the back with a paler inner bowl. Widen the muzzle to a canine wedge (deep at the stop, blunt at the nose), add a black mask from the nose to the eye and a black midline stripe over the crown.

rows.readsAs: a white llama-shaped thing wearing a wet mop
rows.headWhy: A long smooth white wedge with a big round eye and the same two-leaf ear pair everything else in this batch is wearing (here just shorter and greyer). It is nearly interchangeable with the Arctic Fox head — both are white tapering wedges with a dot nose and a long straight mouth seam. Nothing says camelid: no blunt cropped muzzle, no split upper lip, no topknot.
rows.defect: (a) The fleece is drawn as long STRAIGHT parallel bristles that project outward past the body outline and hang below the belly like a grass skirt, while the body surface underneath stays smooth and bald — dense crimped wool reads as volume, not as spikes on a smooth solid. The head, neck top and legs are completely bare, so the coat looks stuck on rather than grown. (b) The face is a long tapered wedge; the reference calls for a blunt short face and it is not there. (c) The tail is a flat hard-edged grey CIRCLE pasted on the rump, sticking off the back edge like a sticker.
rows.fix: Convert the fleece from outward spikes to volume: inflate the body silhouette by the fleece depth and break that silhouette with small crimped clumps (short arcs, varied direction) rather than long straight radial hairs; carry the fleece up the neck and onto the crown as a topknot fringe that overhangs the brow, and stop it cleanly at a bare lower leg. Shorten the muzzle by ~35% and square off its end, add a split upper lip and a small nostril slit. Replace the disc with a short fleece-covered tail that reads as a continuation of the rump curve, not a separate circle.

rows.readsAs: a teal cartoon deer
rows.headWhy: The lyre horns carry it — they are a genuine species marker and no other head in this batch could be swapped in without the horns going missing. But the horns are doing all the work: the skull under them is the same narrow wedge with a straight mouth seam as the Aardvark, Alpaca and Arctic Fox, and the ear is a barely visible leaf tucked behind the horn base.
rows.defect: (a) Body colour is saturated teal/cyan with no white belly — the reference specifies tan flank with a white belly, and every other Earth mammal in the batch is naturalistic, so this reads as an alien reskin rather than an antelope. (b) The tail is a hard-edged dark teal CIRCLE on the rump, the same disc artifact as the Alpaca — the required short flicking tail is not present. (c) The horns are smooth and unringed and their roots sit directly over the eye rather than on the top of the skull behind it. (d) The haunch masses are two soft airbrushed ovals floating on the flank that do not line up with where the legs attach.
rows.fix: Repalette to warm tan over a hard-edged white belly with a dark flank stripe at the boundary. Replace the rump disc with a short tapering tail hanging clear of the body with a dark tip. Add 8-12 raised transverse rings to the lower two-thirds of each horn and move the horn pedicles back onto the crown, behind and above the eye. Re-anchor the shoulder and hip masses so each sits directly over its limb origin and reads as a bulge in the torso outline, not a bruise painted on the side.

rows.readsAs: a seagull's head on a small white pony
rows.headWhy: A featureless white wedge with one flat grey triangle stuck on top of the skull like a shark fin, a long straight top line and a tiny dot nose. It reads AVIAN — a duck or gull bill, not a muzzle. It is interchangeable with the Alpaca head. Nothing vulpine survives: no short blunt muzzle, no cheek ruff, no paired ears.
rows.defect: Three anatomy failures. (1) The muzzle is long, thin and straight-topped — the reference explicitly asks for a BLUNT SHORT muzzle, and the length is what makes the head read as a beak. (2) Only ONE ear is drawn, it is a flat 2D triangle with no bowl, and it is mounted on the crown midline instead of at the rear corner of the skull. (3) NO FEET — the legs are smooth cylinders ending in flat cut-off caps, same as the African Wild Dog. Additionally the tail is a spiky grey-black bristle brush that reads as a broom, where the animal needs a dense ROUND all-white tail.
rows.fix: Cut the muzzle length by half and give it depth: a domed forehead, a short stop, a rounded nose pad, and a fur ruff flaring at the cheeks so the head silhouette is round rather than tapered. Draw two short rounded ears low on the back of the skull with a visible inner bowl and a fur-fringed rim. Add digitigrade paws with a heavy fur pad and stubby toes (the winter foot should look oversized and mitten-like). Rebuild the tail as a fat pure-white cylinder-into-teardrop, roughly torso-depth thick, with soft broken edges instead of straight dark bristles.

rows.readsAs: a striped pig or a painted hyena — nothing armoured
rows.headWhy: It is the Aardvark head, scaled down: same two-leaf brown ear pair, same tiny dot eye, same flat plank snout with a dot nose. There is no armoured head shield, which is the one thing that would make an armadillo head unmistakable, and no small tubular ears as the reference asks for.
rows.defect: The armour does not exist. The bands are flat triangular WEDGE STRIPES painted onto a smooth continuous soft body — no hinge lines, no raised band edges, no shadow between bands, no scapular or pelvic shield, no scute or pebble texture anywhere. The body silhouette is one soft blob with no carapace overhang over the flanks. The tail is a smooth bare cone with no rings, and the feet are the same pale hoof caps as the Aardvark rather than digging claws.
rows.fix: Model the carapace as geometry, not pattern: a solid domed shell whose edge overhangs the flank in the silhouette, split into a front shield, 7-9 hinged mid bands and a rear shield. Give each band a lit top edge and a dark occlusion line beneath it so the hinges read in profile, and stipple each band with rows of small polygonal scutes. Add a triangular scute-covered head shield from the brow to the crown and reduce the ears to two small dark tubes at the shield's rear corners. Ring the tail with 10-12 tapering armour segments. Replace the hoof caps with long curved forefoot digging claws.

rows.readsAs: A shaggy cream sheep with an anteater's beak stuck on the front
rows.headWhy: Structurally identical to the Stoat and Hyena heads: same smooth ovoid cranium, same cone muzzle tapering to a single nostril dot, same small bead eye ringed in bright white sclera. Only the colour differs. Nothing on it says sloth — no flat forward-facing disc face, no dark eye mask, no tiny mouth. Recolour the body and this head would pass as the Stoat's.
rows.defect: Three anatomy failures. (1) FEET: the zoom at x130-270,y220-310 shows four smooth cylindrical legs ending in TWO grey toe caps each — cloven hooves. A sloth's entire read is the long hooked scythe claws; there is not one claw in the picture. (2) SKULL: the muzzle is a long horizontal tapering beak projecting well past the cranium, an anteater/bird profile. A sloth face is flat and round with almost no projection. (3) POSTURE: it stands square on four straight pillars like a barnyard ungulate; the reference explicitly says the limbs should read above the body as it hangs. The shaggy fringe is the only thing doing any work, and it is a fringe of straight spikes hanging off the torso outline rather than coat mapped onto the solid.
rows.fix: Swap the foot primitive from cloven to a curved-claw hook: three long ivory scythes per forelimb, curving back under, drawn as the terminal 40% of the limb so they dominate the silhouette. Collapse the muzzle to headLen*0.15 and round the front of the skull into a flat disc face with the eye set forward on it plus a dark mask patch. Flip the posture: raise the limb attachments above the torso midline so the body slings beneath, or at minimum bend all four limbs into hooks.

rows.readsAs: A grey shaggy capybara or a scruffy donkey foal
rows.headWhy: The long tapering snout with a nose bead at the tip is the same cone the Spectacled Bear, Stoat and Sloth all wear; the only differentiator is a pair of pointed upright leaf ears, and those are wrong for the species anyway (a sloth bear's ears are large, low-set, ragged and floppy, not mule-pointed). Put these ears on the Spectacled Bear and nobody would flag it. The bright white donut sclera around a tiny pupil is also shared batch-wide and reads cartoon, not ursine.
rows.defect: (1) FEET are dark cloven toe caps with a couple of 1px white dashes poking sideways — the huge curved digging claws that define this bear are effectively absent. (2) No shoulder mane: the reference calls for a heavy ruff over the withers and the topline is a smooth even curve with no mass gathered at the shoulder. (3) No pale U/Y chest blaze anywhere; the chest is the same grey as the flank. (4) The body is a mid-grey ticked barrel — this bear is BLACK, and the value is so light it kills the read. (5) The shaggy coat is again straight spikes fringing the outline rather than clumped fur over the volume.
rows.fix: Give it the claw foot, not the cloven foot: five ivory sickles per paw, long enough to be legible at 440px, on a flat plantigrade sole. Darken the base coat to near-black and paint a cream U across the chest. Build an actual mane: add mass to the shoulder silhouette above the withers and let the fur clumps there be 2x the length of the flank clumps. Replace the pointed ears with big, low, round, ragged-edged ones set on the side of the skull below the crown line.

rows.readsAs: A dalmatian-spotted goat, or a white pony with leopard print
